items.title: Bug: Dispatcher proxy() always throws when request body is present
items.body:
The `proxy()` helper inside `Dispatcher.request()` is meant to reject non-JSON requests with a helpful error. The guard is:

```ts
if (body !== undefined && headers.contentType !== "application/json") {
  throw new Error(...);
}
```

The problem is `headers.contentType` (camelCase). HTTP headers use kebab-case (`content-type`), and the `headers` object never has a `contentType` key. `headers.contentType` is always `undefined`, so `undefined !== "application/json"` is always `true`.

The entire condition reduces to `body !== undefined`, meaning the proxy throws for **every** request that carries a body — including valid `application/json` POST requests.

## Failing test

Added in `test/server/dispatcher.proxy.test.ts`:

```
does not throw when proxying a POST request with a JSON body and content-type: application/json
```

Run `yarn test` and look for that test name in the `a dispatcher passes a proxy function to the operation` describe block.

## Root cause

```ts
// src/server/dispatcher.ts
if (body !== undefined && headers.contentType !== "application/json") {
  //                             ^^^^^^^^^^^^^ should be headers["content-type"]
```

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `headers.contentType` is replaced with `headers["content-type"]`
- [ ] The previously failing test passes
- [ ] The existing proxy test continues to pass
- [ ] A POST request with a non-JSON content type is still rejected with the descriptive error

items.title: Bug: Tools.accepts() ignores lowercase 'accept' header — always returns true in production
items.body:
`Tools.accepts()` reads `this.headers.Accept` (capital A). Node.js normalises all incoming HTTP header names to **lowercase**, so when a real HTTP request is processed via Koa the header is stored under `accept` (lowercase). `this.headers.Accept` is therefore always `undefined` in production.

Because `undefined` triggers the early-return guard `if (acceptHeader === "" || acceptHeader === undefined) { return true; }`, the method unconditionally returns `true` — completely ignoring the client's actual Accept header.

## Failing test

Added in `test/server/tools.test.ts`:

```
accepts('application/json') returns false when lowercase 'accept' header is 'text/plain'
```

Run `yarn test` and look for that test name in the `tools` describe block.

## Root cause

```ts
// src/server/tools.ts
const acceptHeader = this.headers.Accept; // ← should be this.headers.accept
```

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `this.headers.Accept` is replaced by a case-insensitive lookup (or lowercased key lookup) so that `accept`, `Accept`, and `ACCEPT` all work
- [ ] The previously failing test passes
- [ ] All other `accepts()` tests continue to pass

items.title: OpenAPI 3.2 — Opportunities for Counterfact
items.body:
## Objective

Break this issue down into subtasks. Do not write any code. 

## Summary 

OpenAPI 3.2 was released in early 2025. This issue identifies changes in the specification and maps each one to a concrete opportunity for Counterfact to adopt it so that Counterfact can be listed as an OpenAPI 3.2 early adopter on [OpenAPI.tools](https://openapi.tools).

The opportunities are grouped by theme and rated by **impact** (how much value it adds to Counterfact users) and **effort** (how much work is required to implement it).

---

## 1. New and Extended HTTP Methods

### 1a. Native `QUERY` method

OpenAPI 3.2 formally adds `query` as a first-class HTTP method alongside `get`, `post`, `put`, `delete`, `options`, `head`, `patch`, and `trace`. The [QUERY method](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-httpbis-safe-method-w-body-02.html) is safe and idempotent but allows a request body, making it useful for complex search/filter operations.

**Current state:** `HttpMethods` in `src/server/registry.ts` and `HTTP_METHODS` in `src/migrate/update-route-types.ts` do not include `QUERY`. The Koa layer, dispatcher, and migration helper would all need updating.

**Opportunity:** Add `"QUERY"` to `HttpMethods`, `ALL_HTTP_METHODS`, and the migration helper's `HTTP_METHODS` list. The code generator already iterates over all keys in a path definition, so generation would work automatically once the server recognises the method.

**Impact:** Medium — Enables mock servers for APIs that use the QUERY method  
**Effort:** Low — Small, mechanical additions to a handful of files

### 1b. Arbitrary methods via `additionalOperations`

For HTTP methods that do not have a dedicated field in the Path Item Object (e.g. `LINK`, `UNLINK`, `LOCK`), OpenAPI 3.2 introduces an `additionalOperations` key. Values are Operation Objects keyed by the method name in its correct capitalisation.

**Current state:** The generator in `src/typescript-generator/generate.ts` iterates over all top-level keys in each path item, so keys like `get`, `post`, etc. are processed automatically. However, `additionalOperations` is a *nested* object and would not be unwrapped by the current loop; those operations would be silently ignored.

**Opportunity:** Detect the `additionalOperations` key during code generation and flatten its entries into the same processing loop. The server layer would also need to forward requests with custom method names to the matching handler.

**Impact:** Low–Medium — Niche use cases but required for full 3.2 compliance  
**Effort:** Medium — Requires changes to the generator loop and the Koa/dispatcher layer

---

## 2. Streaming and Sequential Media Types

OpenAPI 3.2 introduces first-class support for streaming responses via sequential media types such as `text/event-stream` (Server-Sent Events), `multipart/mixed`, `application/jsonl`, and `application/json-seq`. A new `itemSchema` field in the Media Type Object describes the schema of each individual item in the stream, while responses are conceptually treated as arrays of schema instances.

**Current state:** Counterfact generates typed response builders and can return example data from the spec, but has no concept of streaming or server-sent events. The `text/event-stream` content type is not specially handled.

**Opportunity:**

- Recognise `itemSchema` in `src/typescript-generator/schema-type-coder.ts` / `src/typescript-generator/response-type-coder.ts` and generate `Array<T>` types for it.
- In the server layer, when a request accepts `text/event-stream`, send an SSE-formatted response (using Node.js streams) instead of a one-shot JSON body.
- Expose a helper on the `$` argument (similar to `$.proxy`) that allows route handlers to push events to a stream.

**Impact:** High — SSE is widely used in modern APIs (AI/LLM streaming, real-time dashboards)  
**Effort:** High — Requires new server streaming infrastructure and type-generation changes

---

## 3. `querystring` Parameter Location

OpenAPI 3.2 adds `querystring` as a new value for the `in` field of a Parameter Object. Unlike the existing `query` (which targets a single named query parameter), `querystring` treats the entire query string as a single field and allows it to be parsed with a schema, similar to how `requestBody` works for request bodies.

**Current state:** `src/typescript-generator/parameters-type-coder.ts` generates typed objects for `query`, `path`, `header`, and `cookie` parameters. A `querystring` parameter would be ignored.

**Opportunity:** Handle `in: querystring` in `ParametersTypeCoder` and in the dispatcher's parameter-extraction logic. Generate a typed `querystring` property on the `$` argument.

**Impact:** Medium — Simplifies complex query-string APIs (e.g. OData, OpenSearch)  
**Effort:** Medium — Requires changes to both the type generator and the server dispatcher

---

## 4. Example Object — `dataValue` and `serializedValue`

The Example Object gains two new fields:

- `dataValue` — the example expressed as a structured (parsed) value, analogous to the existing `value` field.
- `serializedValue` — the example as it would appear on the wire, as a string.

The existing `externalValue` is now explicitly documented as a serialized value.

**Current state:** Counterfact's random-response logic reads the `value` field from Example Objects when returning example responses.

**Opportunity:**

- Prefer `dataValue` over `value` when generating example responses so that structured data is used correctly.
- Optionally support `serializedValue` for content types where the wire format differs from the parsed form (e.g. `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`).

**Impact:** Medium — Improves correctness of example responses for APIs that use the new fields  
**Effort:** Low — A small change in the response-building / example-selection logic

---

## 5. Discriminator Improvements

### 5a. Optional `propertyName`

The `discriminator.propertyName` field is now optional. When absent, a `defaultMapping` (see below) must be provided.

**Current state:** `SchemaTypeCoder.writeGroup()` relies on `allOf`/`anyOf`/`oneOf` without inspecting the `discriminator` object; `propertyName` being absent would not cause an error but the generated union type would be unchanged.

**Opportunity:** No immediate breaking change; ensure that the absence of `propertyName` does not cause a runtime error during type generation.

**Impact:** Low  
**Effort:** Low — Defensive null-check only

### 5b. `defaultMapping`

A new `defaultMapping` field on the Discriminator Object specifies which schema to use when `propertyName` is absent or the value is not found in `mapping`.

**Opportunity:** Use `defaultMapping` in `SchemaTypeCoder` to emit a more accurate union type when generating TypeScript, including the default variant.

**Impact:** Low–Medium — Improves accuracy of generated types for polymorphic schemas  
**Effort:** Low — Small addition to `SchemaTypeCoder.writeGroup()`

---

## 6. Tag Enhancements

Tags gain three new fields:

- `summary` — a short title for the tag, used in lists.
- `parent` — points to a parent tag to support nested grouping.
- `kind` — classifies the tag (e.g. `nav`, `audience`). A [public registry](https://spec.openapis.org/registry/tag-kind/index.html) defines conventional values.

**Current state:** Counterfact does not currently process or display tag metadata.

**Opportunity:** The built-in dashboard / Swagger UI page (`src/client/`) could use `summary`, `parent`, and `kind` to render a hierarchical navigation tree, grouping operations by nested tags. This would be particularly valuable for large APIs.

**Impact:** Medium — Improves discoverability in the built-in UI for large APIs  
**Effort:** Medium — Frontend work in the Handlebars/Vue layer

---

## 7. Response Object Changes

### 7a. `description` is now optional

Previously, the Response Object required `description`. In 3.2 it is optional.

**Current state:** The generator does not validate or use `description`. Missing descriptions would not cause an error in the current code.

**Opportunity:** No code changes needed; confirm in the test suite that an operation with responses that have no `description` is handled gracefully.

**Impact:** Low — Correctness / robustness improvement  
**Effort:** Very Low — Add a test case

### 7b. New `summary` field on responses

A short `summary` field is now supported alongside `description` on Response Objects.

**Opportunity:** Surface `summary` in the built-in API-testing UI (`src/client/api-tester.html.hbs`) as a tooltip or label when listing available response codes.

**Impact:** Low — Minor UX improvement  
**Effort:** Low

---

## 8. Security Scheme Updates

### 8a. OAuth2 Device Authorization flow

The OAuth2 Security Scheme Flows Object gains a `deviceAuthorization` entry with a `deviceAuthorizationUrl` field (per [RFC 8628](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8628)).

**Current state:** Counterfact's `OperationTypeCoder` checks for `type === "http" && scheme === "basic"` to determine the `user` type on the `$` argument. Other flows are not specially handled.

**Opportunity:** Recognise `deviceAuthorization` flow in `OperationTypeCoder` so that the generated handler type includes the correct credential shape for device-flow tokens.

**Impact:** Low–Medium — Niche but growing use case (CLI tools, smart TVs)  
**Effort:** Low

### 8b. `oauth2MetadataUrl`

A new top-level field on the OAuth2 Security Scheme provides the URL of the authorisation server's metadata document (per [RFC 8414](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8414)).

**Opportunity:** Display this URL in the built-in dashboard to help developers configure OAuth2 clients against the mock server.

**Impact:** Low  
**Effort:** Low

### 8c. `deprecated` on security schemes

Security schemes can now be marked `deprecated: true`.

**Opportunity:** Emit a TypeScript `@deprecated` JSDoc comment in the generated handler types when the security scheme used by an operation is deprecated.

**Impact:** Low — Surfaces specification intent to developers as a compiler warning  
**Effort:** Low

---

## 9. `$self` — Document Identity and URL Resolution

A new top-level `$self` field allows an OpenAPI document to declare its own canonical URI, which is used as the base when resolving relative `$ref` values.

**Current state:** Counterfact uses `@apidevtools/json-schema-ref-parser` for bundling, which already handles base-URI resolution. The `$self` field would be passed through.

**Opportunity:** Ensure that the spec loader in `src/typescript-generator/specification.ts` and `src/server/openapi-middleware.ts` does not strip or misinterpret `$self` when bundling. Add a test with a spec that uses `$self` to verify correct `$ref` resolution.

**Impact:** Low — Mainly a correctness/robustness guarantee  
**Effort:** Very Low — Likely already works; add a regression test

---

## 10. `mediaTypes` Component

A new `mediaTypes` key is supported under `components` to allow reuse of Media Type Objects (similar to how `schemas`, `responses`, `parameters`, and `examples` are reused today).

**Current state:** `src/typescript-generator/generate.ts` only reads `#/paths` and `#/components/securitySchemes`. Other component types are resolved via `$ref` by the bundler.

**Opportunity:** Ensure that `$ref` values pointing to `#/components/mediaTypes/...` are resolved correctly at both code-generation time and at runtime. The bundler likely handles this automatically; add a test to confirm.

**Impact:** Low — Reuse of media type definitions is a DX improvement for API designers  
**Effort:** Very Low — Likely already works via `$ref` bundling; add a test

---

## 11. XML `nodeType` Field

A new `nodeType` field on the XML Object maps a schema to an XML node type: `element`, `attribute`, `text`, `cdata`, or `none`. `attribute: true` is deprecated in favour of `nodeType: attribute`, and `wrapped: true` is deprecated in favour of `nodeType: element`.

**Current state:** Counterfact has a `src/server/json-to-xml.ts` helper for XML serialisation, but it is not clear how much of the XML Object is currently supported.

**Opportunity:** Update `json-to-xml.ts` to understand `nodeType` and treat the deprecated `attribute: true` / `wrapped: true` fields as synonyms during the transition period.

**Impact:** Low — Relevant only to XML-based APIs  
**Effort:** Medium — Requires understanding and updating the XML serialisation logic

---

## 12. Server Object `name` Field

The Server Object gains a `name` field alongside the existing `description`, `url`, and `variables` fields.

**Current state:** `src/server/openapi-middleware.ts` injects a `Counterfact` server entry with only `description` and `url`.

**Opportunity:** Set `name: "Counterfact"` in the injected server entry so that tools that display `name` (including OpenAPI 3.2-aware UIs) render it correctly.

**Impact:** Low — Minor UX improvement in Swagger UI and similar tools  
**Effort:** Very Low — One-line change in `openapi-middleware.ts`

---

## 13. JSON Schema Alignment

OpenAPI 3.2 updates its embedded JSON Schema reference to [draft-bhutton-json-schema-01](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-bhutton-json-schema-01.html) and [draft-bhutton-json-schema-validation-01](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-bhutton-json-schema-validation-01.html).

**Current state:** Counterfact uses `json-schema-faker` for generating random values from schemas. The library's supported draft determines what schema keywords are available.

**Opportunity:** Verify that `json-schema-faker` supports the keywords introduced in `draft-bhutton-json-schema-01` (notably the revised `unevaluatedProperties`, `unevaluatedItems`, and `prefixItems`). Upgrade the library or add workarounds as necessary.

**Impact:** Medium — Affects correctness of random response generation  
**Effort:** Low–Medium — Depends on the library's current support level

---

## Summary Table

| Opportunity | Impact | Effort | Files Affected |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1a. `QUERY` HTTP method | Medium | Low | `registry.ts`, `update-route-types.ts`, `koa-middleware.ts` |
| 1b. `additionalOperations` | Low–Medium | Medium | `generate.ts`, `dispatcher.ts`, `registry.ts` |
| 2. Streaming / SSE (`itemSchema`) | High | High | `response-type-coder.ts`, `schema-type-coder.ts`, `koa-middleware.ts`, new streaming helper |
| 3. `querystring` parameter | Medium | Medium | `parameters-type-coder.ts`, `dispatcher.ts` |
| 4. `dataValue`/`serializedValue` examples | Medium | Low | Response/example selection logic |
| 5a. Optional discriminator `propertyName` | Low | Low | `schema-type-coder.ts` |
| 5b. Discriminator `defaultMapping` | Low–Medium | Low | `schema-type-coder.ts` |
| 6. Tag `summary`/`parent`/`kind` | Medium | Medium | `src/client/` templates |
| 7a. Optional response `description` | Low | Very Low | Test only |
| 7b. Response `summary` | Low | Low | `src/client/api-tester.html.hbs` |
| 8a. OAuth2 Device Authorization flow | Low–Medium | Low | `operation-type-coder.ts` |
| 8b. `oauth2MetadataUrl` | Low | Low | `src/client/` templates |
| 8c. `deprecated` security scheme | Low | Low | `operation-type-coder.ts` |
| 9. `$self` document identity | Low | Very Low | Test only |
| 10. `mediaTypes` component | Low | Very Low | Test only |
| 11. XML `nodeType` | Low | Medium | `json-to-xml.ts` |
| 12. Server `name` field | Low | Very Low | `openapi-middleware.ts` |
| 13. JSON Schema alignment | Medium | Low–Medium | `json-schema-faker` usage |

---

## Recommended Starting Points

If the goal is to be listed as an **early adopter** with minimal investment, the highest-return items are:

1. **`QUERY` HTTP method (1a)** — High visibility, low effort, clearly demonstrates 3.2 awareness.
2. **`dataValue`/`serializedValue` examples (4)** — Simple change with user-visible impact on example responses.
3. **Server `name` field (12)** — Trivial change that shows up in every OpenAPI-aware UI.
4. **Streaming / SSE (2)** — High user demand; worth investing in even though it requires more work.
5. **`querystring` parameter (3)** — Useful for complex search/filter APIs; moderate effort.

---

items.title: Add CI workflow to create GitHub issues from proposed issue files + update copilot-instructions.md
items.body:
## Title
Add CI workflow to create sub-issues from Markdown proposal files and move issue-authoring instructions into a dedicated file

## Summary

We want a safe, reviewable workflow for issue creation.

Instead of allowing Copilot to create GitHub issues directly, we will:

1. Allow Copilot to propose issues as Markdown files in the repo
2. Review those files in a pull request
3. Use a GitHub Action to create real GitHub issues after merge
4. Make each created issue a sub-issue of the issue Copilot is currently implementing
5. Delete the proposal files after successful creation, following the general pattern used by Changesets
6. Move issue-authoring guidance into a dedicated instructions file referenced by `copilot-instructions.md`

This keeps credentials out of the agent runtime, preserves human review, and supports hierarchical planning.

## Requirements

### 1. Proposed issue file location

Create a convention for issue proposal files, for example:

```text
.github/issue-proposals/*.md
```

Each file represents one proposed GitHub issue.

Do not use `.github/issues/`, since that can be confused with GitHub issue templates.

### 2. File format

Use Markdown files with YAML front matter for metadata.

Example:

```md
---
title: Add JSDocs to generated types
parentIssue: 1234
labels:
  - enhancement
  - generator
assignees: []
milestone:
---

Generate JSDoc comments for emitted TypeScript types using metadata from the OpenAPI spec.

## Acceptance criteria

- Description fields map to JSDoc where available
- Parameter and schema docs are preserved
- Generated output remains valid TypeScript
```

Rules:

- Front matter is required
- `title` is required
- Body content after the front matter becomes the GitHub issue body
- `labels`, `assignees`, and `milestone` are optional
- `parentIssue` should be included in front matter by Copilot, but CI should not require it

### 3. Parent issue / sub-issue behavior

Each created issue must be created as a sub-issue of the issue the agent is currently implementing.

Preferred convention:
- include an explicit `parentIssue` field in front matter so the relationship is visible and auditable in the file itself

However, the CI workflow must not require `parentIssue` to be present in the proposal file.

Instead, the workflow should determine the parent issue using repository context, such as the issue associated with the pull request or branch being merged. If `parentIssue` is present, the workflow may use it as a hint or validation aid, but the source of truth should be the workflow’s derived parent context.

If the workflow cannot determine the parent issue for a proposal file, fail processing for that file and do not delete it.

### 4. GitHub Action

Create a workflow at:

```text
.github/workflows/create-issues.yml
```

Behavior:

- Trigger on push to `main` when files under `.github/issue-proposals/*.md` change
- For each Markdown proposal file:
  - Parse front matter
  - Validate required fields
  - Use the Markdown body as the issue body
  - Determine the parent issue from repository context
  - Create a GitHub issue
  - Associate it as a sub-issue of the resolved parent issue
  - Apply labels if provided
  - Apply assignees if provided
  - Apply milestone if provided and resolvable

Use the repository token:

```yaml
GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
```

Use the GitHub API or `gh` CLI, whichever is simpler and more reliable for sub-issue creation.

### 5. Cleanup after creation

After a proposal file is successfully converted into a GitHub issue, delete the file from `.github/issue-proposals/`.

This should follow the general pattern of Changesets:

- proposal files live in the repo while under review
- merge to `main` triggers processing
- successful processing removes the consumed file

Implementation note:
- the workflow should commit the deletion back to the repository after successful issue creation

### 6. Failure behavior

If issue creation fails for any file:

- do not delete that file
- fail the workflow
- leave the file in place so it can be retried after the problem is fixed

### 7. Validation

Fail the workflow if:

- front matter is missing
- front matter is invalid YAML
- `title` is missing or empty
- body content is empty
- the workflow cannot determine a parent issue from repository context

Do not fail merely because `parentIssue` is missing from front matter.

### 8. Move instructions into a dedicated file

Create a dedicated instructions file for issue proposal authoring, for example:

```text
.github/instructions/issue-proposals.instructions.md
```

This file should define:

• where issue proposal files go  
• the required Markdown + front matter format  
• required and optional fields  
• that proposals are intended to become sub-issues of the current parent issue  
• that Copilot should include `parentIssue` in front matter when possible, even though CI does not require it  
• that Copilot must never attempt direct issue creation via API or browser automation  
• expectations for issue quality, including context and acceptance criteria

Then update `copilot-instructions.md` so it references this file rather than embedding all of the issue-authoring rules inline.

The goal is to keep `copilot-instructions.md` concise and make the issue workflow reusable and easier to maintain.

### 9. Update copilot-instructions.md

Update `copilot-instructions.md` so Copilot:

- references the dedicated issue proposal instructions file
- never attempts to create issues directly via API or browser automation
- always proposes issues as Markdown files under `.github/issue-proposals/`
- uses YAML front matter for metadata
- includes `parentIssue` when possible
- writes clear issue bodies with:
  - summary/context
  - motivation
  - acceptance criteria

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Markdown-based issue proposal format exists under `.github/issue-proposals/*.md`
- [ ] Front matter is parsed and validated
- [ ] Workflow exists at `.github/workflows/create-issues.yml`
- [ ] Workflow creates GitHub issues from valid proposal files
- [ ] Workflow determines the parent issue from repository context
- [ ] Workflow associates each created issue as a sub-issue of the resolved parent issue
- [ ] Workflow applies labels and assignees when provided
- [ ] Workflow attempts milestone assignment when provided
- [ ] Successfully processed proposal files are deleted automatically
- [ ] Failed proposal files remain in the repo
- [ ] Dedicated issue-authoring instructions file exists
- [ ] `copilot-instructions.md` references that file
- [ ] Copilot no longer attempts direct issue creation

## Example proposal file

```md
---
title: Add JSDocs to generated types
parentIssue: 1234
labels:
  - enhancement
  - generator
assignees: []
milestone:
---

Generate JSDoc comments for emitted TypeScript types using metadata from the OpenAPI spec.

## Acceptance criteria

- Description fields map to JSDoc where available
- Parameter and schema docs are preserved
- Generated output remains valid TypeScript
```

## Notes for implementation

- Prefer a simple implementation over a clever one
- Keep dependencies minimal
- A small script checked into the repo is fine if it makes the workflow easier to read and test
- The workflow should be able to process multiple issue files in one run
- The commit that deletes processed files should be clearly attributable to the workflow
- The sub-issue linkage should be implemented in a way that is robust and testable
- `parentIssue` in front matter is for clarity and authoring guidance, not as a hard CI requirement

## Why this matters

- Keeps credentials out of agent runtime
- Makes issue creation reviewable through pull requests
- Preserves a clean audit trail
- Supports parent/child planning
- Keeps the repo tidy by removing consumed proposal files
- Keeps Copilot guidance modular and maintainable

items.title: Tell Copilot to use TDD
items.body:
Here are some new instructions. Integrate them into copilot-instructions.md and remove any existing instructions that would be redundant. 

## Test-driven workflow

When implementing a change, work in a test-first or test-guided way whenever practical.

### Default workflow

1. Understand the requested behavior before changing code.
2. Identify the smallest observable behavior that proves the change works.
3. Add or update automated tests for that behavior first.
4. Run the relevant tests and confirm they fail for the expected reason when feasible.
5. Implement the smallest code change needed to make the tests pass.
6. Refactor only after the tests are green.
7. Run all relevant tests again before finishing.

### Expectations

- Prefer adding tests at the level that best captures user-visible behavior.
- Do not change tests merely to accommodate broken behavior unless the requested behavior has changed.
- Do not remove tests without explaining why.
- Avoid over-mocking. Prefer realistic behavior and real integration boundaries where practical.
- Keep tests readable. A test should make it obvious what behavior is expected.
- Cover at least:
  - the main success path
  - one meaningful edge case
  - one regression risk when applicable

### When to add tests

Add or update tests for:
- bug fixes
- new features
- refactors that could change behavior
- generated code, when generation behavior is being changed
- any change that affects external contracts, APIs, schemas, or CLI behavior

### When tests are hard to add

If a test is difficult to write:
1. Do not skip testing silently.
2. Explain why the code is hard to test.
3. Improve the design if possible to make testing easier.
4. If automated coverage is still impractical, provide clear manual verification steps.

### Definition of done

A change is not complete until:
- the relevant tests exist
- the relevant tests pass
- the implementation matches the requested behavior
- manual verification steps are included when needed

### Manual acceptance tests

For every pull request, include a section titled:

Manual acceptance tests

Under that section, provide 3 to 6 unchecked checkboxes describing observable behaviors a human can verify manually. These should include:
- the primary success case
- at least one edge case
- at least one regression check

Example:

- [ ] Creating a pet with a valid payload returns 201
- [ ] Creating a pet with a missing required field returns 400
- [ ] Existing pet lookup behavior still works after the change

### Decision rule

When choosing between:
- writing more production code
- tightening tests
- simplifying design

prefer the option that improves feedback quality and reduces ambiguity.

If you want, I can also give you a version tailored specifically for Counterfact.

items.title: Add JSDocs
items.body:
# Add JSDoc generation for types from OpenAPI metadata

## Summary
Generated TypeScript types currently lack inline documentation.

This makes it harder for developers (and AI agents) to understand how to use the generated API surface without constantly referencing the OpenAPI spec.

We should enrich generated types with JSDoc comments derived from the OpenAPI document.

## Problem
Counterfact already uses the OpenAPI spec as the source of truth for structure and validation.

However, important descriptive metadata is being discarded during generation:
- `description`
- `summary`
- `example` / `examples`
- `deprecated`
- `format`
- `default`
- `enum` descriptions (if present via extensions)

This results in:
- Poor IDE autocomplete experience (no hover info)
- Reduced usability for humans
- Reduced effectiveness for AI agents (less semantic context)
- Increased need to cross-reference the spec manually

## Proposal
Enhance the type generator to emit JSDoc comments using available OpenAPI metadata.

### Example

**OpenAPI input**
```yaml
components:
  schemas:
    Pet:
      type: object
      description: A pet in the store
      properties:
        id:
          type: integer
          description: Unique identifier for the pet
          example: 123
        name:
          type: string
          description: The pet's name
```

**Generated output**
```ts
/**
 * A pet in the store
 */
export interface Pet {
  /**
   * Unique identifier for the pet
   * @example 123
   */
  id: number;

  /**
   * The pet's name
   */
  name: string;
}
```

## Scope

### 1. Schema-level docs
- Add JSDoc to interfaces/types from:
  - `description`
  - `summary` (fallback if no description)

### 2. Property-level docs
- Include:
  - `description`
  - `example` / first entry from `examples`
  - `default`
  - `format` (optional tag or inline note)
  - `deprecated` → `@deprecated`

### 3. Operation-level types
- Apply JSDoc to:
  - request types
  - response types
  - route handlers (if applicable)

Use:
- `summary` as first line
- `description` as extended text

### 4. Enum support
- Add inline comments for enum values when metadata is available
- Consider support for `x-enum-descriptions` (common extension)

### 5. Tags
Where appropriate, include:
- `@example`
- `@default`
- `@deprecated`
- `@remarks` (for longer descriptions if needed)

## Design Considerations

### Formatting
- Keep output clean and readable
- Avoid overly verbose comments
- Trim excessive whitespace and markdown from OpenAPI input
- Preserve line breaks where useful

### Safety
- Escape characters that would break JSDoc (`*/`, etc.)
- Handle missing or malformed metadata gracefully

### Determinism
- Generated output should be stable for the same spec
- Avoid non-deterministic ordering of examples or fields

## AI-Specific Benefits
This significantly improves Counterfact’s usefulness for AI-driven workflows:
- Provides semantic hints directly in the type system
- Reduces need for external spec parsing
- Improves prompt grounding when agents read code
- Enables better code completion and reasoning

## Acceptance Criteria
- Generated types include JSDoc comments from OpenAPI metadata
- IDE hover shows meaningful descriptions and examples
- No breaking changes to existing type structure
- Output remains deterministic
- Handles missing metadata without errors

items.title: Add lightweight telemetry using PostHog (initial usage tracking)
items.body:
## Summary
We want to add minimal telemetry to understand how many people are actually using Counterfact.

At this stage, we are **not** trying to analyze behavior deeply.  
We only want a simple, reliable signal of usage.

## Goal
Track how many unique environments are running Counterfact.

## Scope (keep this intentionally small)
- Integrate PostHog
- Track a single event: `counterfact_started`

## Requirements

### 1. Install PostHog
- Add PostHog Node SDK to the project

### 2. Configure PostHog client

Use a hardcoded project API key (public ingest key).

```ts
const POSTHOG_API_KEY = 'phc_msXmBxiL8FVugNMLCx9bnPQGqfEMc';
const POSTHOG_HOST = 'https://app.posthog.com';
```

- This key is safe to include in CLI code (it is not a secret)
- Do NOT require users to provide a key
- Do NOT block startup if configuration is missing

Optional override (for testing/flexibility):

```ts
const key = process.env.POSTHOG_API_KEY ?? POSTHOG_API_KEY;
const host = process.env.POSTHOG_HOST ?? POSTHOG_HOST;
```

### 3. Emit event on startup

Event name:
- `counterfact_started`

Properties:
- `version` (Counterfact version)
- `nodeVersion`
- `platform` (process.platform)
- `arch` (process.arch)
- `source: 'counterfact-cli'`

### 4. Anonymous identity
- Generate a random UUID per run (no persistence required for now)
- Use this as `distinct_id`

We are NOT trying to track users across sessions yet.

### 5. Non-blocking behavior
- Telemetry must NEVER block startup
- Fire-and-forget (do not await)
- Fail silently if PostHog is unreachable

### 6. Never run telemetry in CI

Telemetry must not run in CI under any circumstances.

Requirements:
- If `process.env.CI` is set to a truthy value, do not send telemetry
- Suppress the pre-rollout warning in CI as well
- CI should win over all other rules

### 7. Opt-out / control behavior

Telemetry behavior depends on date and env var:

- In CI
  - Telemetry is always disabled

- Before **May 1, 2026**
  - Telemetry is **disabled by default**
  - Telemetry is only enabled if:
    - `COUNTERFACT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=false`

- On or after **May 1, 2026**
  - Telemetry is **enabled by default**
  - Telemetry can be disabled with:
    - `COUNTERFACT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=true`

### 8. Startup warning (pre-rollout)

Before May 1, 2026, display a one-line warning on startup:

```text
Telemetry will be enabled by default starting May 1, 2026. Learn more and how to disable: https://counterfact.dev/telemetry
```

Requirements:
- Show once per run (no persistence needed)
- Do not show if:
  - `COUNTERFACT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=true`
  - running in CI
- Keep it concise and non-intrusive

### 9. Keep it lightweight
- No abstractions
- No wrappers beyond what is necessary
- This is intentionally minimal

## Example (rough shape)

```ts
import { PostHog } from 'posthog-node';
import { randomUUID } from 'node:crypto';

const POSTHOG_API_KEY = 'phc_your_project_api_key_here';
const POSTHOG_HOST = 'https://app.posthog.com';

const key = process.env.POSTHOG_API_KEY ?? POSTHOG_API_KEY;
const host = process.env.POSTHOG_HOST ?? POSTHOG_HOST;

const isCI = Boolean(process.env.CI);
const isBeforeRollout = new Date() < new Date('2026-05-01');
const disabledEnv = process.env.COUNTERFACT_TELEMETRY_DISABLED;

const isDisabled =
  isCI ||
  disabledEnv === 'true' ||
  (isBeforeRollout && disabledEnv !== 'false');

if (!isDisabled) {
  const client = new PostHog(key, { host });

  client.capture({
    distinctId: randomUUID(),
    event: 'counterfact_started',
    properties: {
      version,
      nodeVersion: process.version,
      platform: process.platform,
      arch: process.arch,
      source: 'counterfact-cli',
    },
  });
}

if (!isCI && isBeforeRollout && disabledEnv !== 'true') {
  console.warn(
    'Telemetry will be enabled by default starting May 1, 2026. Learn more and how to disable: https://counterfact.dev/telemetry'
  );
}
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] PostHog is installed and configured
- [ ] API key is defined with placeholder value
- [ ] Optional env var overrides are supported
- [ ] `counterfact_started` event fires according to rollout rules
- [ ] Event includes required properties
- [ ] Telemetry does not block startup
- [ ] Telemetry never runs in CI
- [ ] Warning is never shown in CI
- [ ] Telemetry respects env var and rollout date
- [ ] Warning is shown before May 1, 2026
- [ ] Warning is suppressed when telemetry is disabled
- [ ] No errors are surfaced to the user if telemetry fails

## Out of Scope (for now)

- Persistent user identity
- Feature-level tracking
- Funnels or analytics dashboards
- OpenTelemetry integration

## Notes

This is step one.

We are only trying to answer:
> “Is anyone using this?”

Do not over-engineer this.

items.title: A syntax error in a route file should not cause Counterfact to crash
items.body:
If a file under `./routes` has a syntax error, Counterfact currently crashes. 

The server should not crash. Requests to that route should return a 500 error with a message: "There is a syntax error in the route file: ./routes/my/path.ts"

Hi there,

I am working with `counterfact@2.4.0` and I encountered a problem where the OpenAPI spec defines an endpoint with an `operationId` that is a reserved keyword (like `delete`). Take following spec as an example and try to run it:

```

  title: Example - OpenAPI 3.1
  version: 0.0.1
paths:
  /stuff/{stuffId}:
    delete:
      operationId: delete
      parameters: 
        - name: stuffId
          in: path
          required: true
          schema:
            type: string
      responses:
        '204':
          description: successful deletion

```

This results in following error:

```
SyntaxError: Identifier expected. (1:15)
> 1 | import type { delete } from "../../types/paths/stuff/{stuffId}.types.js";
    |               ^
  2 |
  3 | export const DELETE:delete = async ($) => {
  4 |         return $.response[204];

```

Perhaps it is somehow possible to mask such `operationIds`?

Thank you! :)

items.title: Ensure users running via `npx` are using the latest version
items.body:
### Problem

Users running Counterfact via `npx` may unknowingly execute a cached or outdated version of the package.

Example:

```
npx counterfact <openapi-url>
```

Because `npx` caches previously downloaded versions, users may not automatically receive the latest release—even after we publish updates.

This creates a few risks:

- Users experience bugs that have already been fixed
- Behavior differs from documentation or examples
- Reduced confidence in the tool (“this doesn’t work as expected”)
- Harder to support, since version is often unknown

---

### Goal

Make it easy (and natural) for users to run the latest version, and make it obvious when they are not.

---

### Proposed Solution

#### 1. Recommend `@latest` in all docs and examples

Update all documentation and examples to use:

```
npx counterfact@latest <openapi-url>
```

This ensures version resolution always targets the latest published version.

---

#### 2. Add runtime version check

On CLI startup:

- Detect current version (`package.json`)
- Fetch latest version from npm registry
- Compare versions
- If outdated, print a non-blocking warning

Example:

```
You're running counterfact 1.3.0
Latest version is 1.4.2

Run: npx counterfact@latest
```

This addresses the human problem directly.

---

#### 3. Display current version on startup

Always print the current version in CLI output (or in verbose mode), so users and maintainers can quickly identify what is running.

---

#### 4. Provide opt-out for CI / automation

Add a flag to disable version checks:

```
--no-update-check
```

Or automatically suppress in CI environments.

---

### Optional Enhancements

- Add support for dist-tags (e.g., `@beta`) for early adopters
- Add telemetry (opt-in) to understand version distribution
- Include version info in bug report templates

---

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] All docs and examples use `npx counterfact@latest`
- [ ] CLI prints current version at startup
- [ ] CLI checks for latest version and warns if outdated
- [ ] Warning includes exact command to upgrade
- [ ] Version check can be disabled (flag or CI detection)

---

### Notes

We cannot control `npx` caching behavior, but we can:

- Encourage correct usage (`@latest`)
- Surface version drift clearly
- Reduce support friction

This aligns with Counterfact’s philosophy: predictable, observable, and explicit behavior.

items.title: Counterfact Landing Pages — Prioritized Audience List
items.body:
This is an AI generated prioritized list of landing pages based on:

- clarity of pain
- existing demand
- ease of conversion
- strategic leverage (category positioning)

Each section includes:
- audience
- core pain
- why it matters
- positioning angle

---

## Tier 1 — Highest Leverage (Build First)

### 1. Mock Server Users (Postman, WireMock, MSW, etc.)

**Audience:**  
People using mock servers today

**Core Pain:**  
Mocks start simple but become brittle, drift from reality, and require constant maintenance

**Why It Matters:**  
They already believe in the problem and are actively looking for a better solution

**Positioning Angle:**  
Mocks return data. Counterfact simulates systems.

---

### 2. UI Developers Waiting on Backend

**Audience:**  
Frontend engineers blocked by missing or unstable APIs

**Core Pain:**  
Blocked progress, fake data hacks, constant rework

**Why It Matters:**  
This is the original use case and still one of the most visceral pains

**Positioning Angle:**  
Build against a real system before the backend exists

---

### 3. Spec Kit / Spec-Driven Development Users

**Audience:**  
People using or exploring GitHub Spec Kit

**Core Pain:**  
Spec defines intent, but there is no reliable system to execute against

**Why It Matters:**  
Rising wave + strong narrative alignment

**Positioning Angle:**  
Spec Kit tells the AI what to build. Counterfact gives it a system to run against.

---

### 4. Agentic Coding (General, not Spec Kit specific)

**Audience:**  
People using Copilot, Claude Code, Cursor, etc.

**Core Pain:**  
AI generates code, but execution is unreliable and environments are inconsistent

**Why It Matters:**  
Fast-growing category with unclear best practices

**Positioning Angle:**  
A deterministic runtime for AI-generated code

---

### 5. QA / E2E Testing (Playwright, Cypress users)

**Audience:**  
Engineers writing end-to-end tests

**Core Pain:**  
Flaky tests, inconsistent environments, unreliable data

**Why It Matters:**  
High pain, high willingness to change tools

**Positioning Angle:**  
Make tests reliable without relying on staging environments

---

## Tier 2 — Strong Expansion (Build Next)

### 6. OpenAPI / API-First Teams

**Audience:**  
Teams already using OpenAPI

**Core Pain:**  
Specs exist but are not executable or enforced in practice

**Why It Matters:**  
Strong alignment with your architecture

**Positioning Angle:**  
Your spec shouldn’t just describe the system. It should be the system.

---

### 7. Postman Users (Disruption Play)

**Audience:**  
Teams using Postman collections and mocks

**Core Pain:**  
Manual workflows, weak state modeling, limited realism

**Why It Matters:**  
Large market, clear dissatisfaction

**Positioning Angle:**  
Stop managing collections. Start simulating systems.

---

### 8. Platform / DevEx Teams

**Audience:**  
Internal tooling, platform engineering, DevEx

**Core Pain:**  
Inconsistent environments, duplicated effort across teams

**Why It Matters:**  
They can drive adoption across an entire org

**Positioning Angle:**  
Standardize how systems are simulated across teams

---

### 9. Backend Engineers

**Audience:**  
API developers and service owners

**Core Pain:**  
Maintaining mocks, contract drift, frontend coordination overhead

**Why It Matters:**  
Often skeptical but influential

**Positioning Angle:**  
Stop writing throwaway mocks. Let the contract drive behavior.

---

### 10. Contract Testing Users (Pact, etc.)

**Audience:**  
Teams using contract testing tools like [Pact](chatgpt://generic-entity?number=0)

**Core Pain:**  
Too many moving parts: contracts, mocks, environments

**Why It Matters:**  
Already bought into the philosophy

**Positioning Angle:**  
Combine contract validation and simulation in one system

---

## Tier 3 — Strategic / Longer-Term

### 11. Executives / Leadership

**Audience:**  
Directors, VPs, CIO-level

**Core Pain:**  
Slow delivery, duplicated environments, high coordination cost

**Why It Matters:**  
Budget and top-down influence

**Positioning Angle:**  
Reduce coordination overhead and accelerate delivery across teams

---

### 12. Non-Developers Entering Agentic Coding

**Audience:**  
PMs, designers, analysts using AI to build software

**Core Pain:**  
No safe environment to experiment, high risk of breaking things

**Why It Matters:**  
Emerging audience

**Positioning Angle:**  
A safe system to build and experiment without backend dependencies

---

### 13. AI Tool Builders / Agent Builders

**Audience:**  
People building AI agents and developer tools

**Core Pain:**  
No safe, controllable runtime for generated code

**Why It Matters:**  
You can become infrastructure for this ecosystem

**Positioning Angle:**  
A sandboxed, deterministic runtime for agents

---

### 14. Integration Engineers

**Audience:**  
Engineers integrating third-party or legacy systems

**Core Pain:**  
Unreliable dependencies, rate limits, inconsistent behavior

**Why It Matters:**  
High friction role with constant blockers

**Positioning Angle:**  
Simulate external systems without depending on them

---

### 15. Startups / Small Teams

**Audience:**  
1–5 engineer teams moving quickly

**Core Pain:**  
Context switching, lack of backend, limited resources

**Why It Matters:**  
Fast adopters, high leverage

**Positioning Angle:**  
Move faster by eliminating backend dependencies early

---

### 16. Data / Analytics Engineers

**Audience:**  
Teams needing consistent data inputs

**Core Pain:**  
Unreliable upstream systems, inconsistent datasets

**Why It Matters:**  
Non-obvious but valuable use case

**Positioning Angle:**  
Generate consistent, contract-driven data sources

---

### 17. Security / Compliance

**Audience:**  
Security and risk stakeholders

**Core Pain:**  
Developers hitting real systems, unsafe test environments

**Why It Matters:**  
Enterprise adoption blocker or accelerator

**Positioning Angle:**  
Test safely without exposing real systems or data

---

### 18. Educators / Bootcamps

**Audience:**  
Teachers and training programs

**Core Pain:**  
Need realistic systems without infrastructure overhead

**Why It Matters:**  
Long-term adoption funnel

**Positioning Angle:**  
Teach full-stack without needing a backend

---

## Meta Personas (Use Across Pages)

### “Future Me”

**Audience:**  
A developer returning to the codebase with limited time

**Core Pain:**  
Context loss, uncertainty, inconsistent systems

**Positioning Angle:**  
A system that behaves predictably every time you come back

---

## Notes

- Each page should start with the audience’s frustration, not the product  
- Avoid describing Counterfact directly until the problem is clearly felt  
- Keep language grounded and specific (no hype, no jargon)  
- Focus on recognition: “this is exactly my problem”

items.title: .apply Command: Environment and Scenario Management
items.body:
### Summary

Introduce a `.apply` command that loads and executes a script to modify the REPL environment.

This enables users to quickly establish known states, compose scenarios, and reuse setup logic across:

- interactive REPL sessions
- agents
- automated tests

The `.apply` command turns the REPL from an ad hoc tool into a **repeatable, composable environment**.

---

## Core Idea

The request builder defines *what to do*.

`.apply` defines *the world in which you do it*.

Example:

```js
.apply pet-store/base
.apply pet-store/sold-pets
```

---

## Capabilities

### 1. Environment Mutation

Apply scripts can modify:

- context (e.g., services, data, flags)
- available builders
- shared configuration (auth, headers, etc.)

---

### 2. Scenario Setup

Scripts can:

- seed data
- reset systems to a known state
- simulate conditions (e.g., failures, edge cases)

Example:

```js
.apply happy-path
.apply error-state
```

---

### 3. Builder Injection

Scripts can add or remove reusable builders.

Example:

```js
getSoldPets.send()
```

These builders are defined inside `.apply` scripts.

---

### 4. Composition and Layering

Scripts can be applied in sequence:

```js
.apply base
.apply auth/admin
.apply pet-store/with-sold-pets
```

Each script may:

- fully reset state
- layer on top of existing state
- override previous changes

---

### 5. Idempotence (Optional)

Scripts may or may not be idempotent.

- Some scripts should be safe to run repeatedly
- Others may intentionally mutate or append state

The system should not enforce one model.

---

## Script Model

Scripts should be **plain TypeScript**, not a custom DSL.

Example:

```js
export default ({ context, builders }) => {
  context.petService.reset();

  context.petService.addPet({ id: 1, status: "sold" });
  context.petService.addPet({ id: 2, status: "available" });

  builders.set(
    "getSoldPets",
    route("/pet/{petId}/findByStatus")
      .method("get")
      .path({ petId: 1 })
      .query({ status: "sold" }),
  );
};
```

---

## Invocation

Support both:

```js
.apply path/to/file.ts
```

and

```js
.apply named-scenario
```

Where named scenarios resolve from configured directories, e.g.:

```
./repl/
./repl-mine/
```

---

## Feedback

After applying a script, the REPL should summarize changes.

Example:

```
Applied pet-store/sold-pets

Context changes:
  petService.reset()
  petService.seededPets = 2

Builders added:
  getSoldPets

Builders removed:
  getPendingPets
```

---

## Design Principles

- Scripts are code, not configuration
- Support both reset and layering models
- Do not require idempotence
- Make changes visible and inspectable
- Enable reuse across REPL, tests, and agents

---

## Big Picture

`.apply` turns the REPL into a:

> **scenario-driven API exploration environment**

Instead of manually setting up state, users can:

- load predefined scenarios
- compose environments incrementally
- share reproducible setups
- use the same scripts across humans, agents, and tests

items.title: Add Agent DSL for Context Operations in REPL
items.body:
## Summary

Introduce an AI-powered `.agent` command in the Counterfact REPL that allows users to express intent in natural language.

The agent translates the request into a **constrained DSL** consisting of explicit operations on the `context` object.

The DSL is:
- **interpreted directly** by Counterfact (no `eval`)
- **validated via generated TypeScript** before execution
- **intentionally limited** to ensure safety, predictability, and debuggability

---

## Goals

- Allow users to manipulate mock state using natural language
- Keep execution safe and deterministic
- Avoid arbitrary code execution
- Leverage existing generated TypeScript types for validation
- Provide clear failure modes and actionable suggestions when capabilities are missing

---

## Non-Goals (v1)

- General-purpose scripting (no loops, variables, conditionals)
- Arbitrary JavaScript execution
- Autonomous agent behavior
- Hidden side effects

---

## Example

### User Input

```
.agent add 10 cats and 20 dogs to the store
```

### Generated DSL (internal)

```
context.store.addPet({ "type": "cat" })
context.store.addPet({ "type": "cat" })
...
context.store.addPet({ "type": "dog" })
```

### Execution Output

```
Executed 30 operations.
Created:
- 10 pets of type "cat"
- 20 pets of type "dog"
```

---

## DSL Design

### Core Principle

The agent produces a **sequence of explicit context operations**, not general-purpose code.

Each line is independently executable.

---

### Allowed Statements

#### 1. Property Assignment

```
context.checkout.fail = true
context.checkout.latencyMs = 2000
```

#### 2. Method Calls

```
context.store.addPet({ "type": "cat" })
context.store.deletePet(42)
```

---

### Allowed Values

- string
- number
- boolean
- null
- object literals
- array literals
- limited helper calls (optional, see below)

---

### Optional Helpers (v1 or later)

Helpers may be allowed in value position only:

```
context.store.addPet({ "name": $petName(), "type": "cat" })
```

These must be:
- pure
- deterministic (or seedable)
- explicitly whitelisted

---

### Not Allowed

- variables (`let`, `const`)
- loops (`for`, `while`)
- conditionals (`if`)
- function declarations
- imports
- `new`, `this`, `eval`
- access outside `context` (except approved helpers)
- computed property access (`context[x]`)
- chaining or indirection

---

## Execution Model

Pipeline:

1. User enters `.agent <instruction>`
2. LLM generates DSL
3. Parse DSL into internal operation list
4. Validate DSL syntax (strict grammar)
5. Generate TypeScript from DSL
6. Type-check against generated `context` types
7. If valid → interpret DSL directly
8. If invalid → return error or suggest patch
9. Summarize execution

---

## Internal Representation

Each statement is normalized into a structured operation:

```json
{ "kind": "call", "path": ["store", "addPet"], "args": [{ "type": "cat" }] }
```

```json
{ "kind": "set", "path": ["checkout", "fail"], "value": true }
```

The interpreter executes this representation directly.

---

## TypeScript Validation

DSL is compiled into a synthetic TypeScript file:

```ts
declare const context: CounterfactContext;

context.store.addPet({ type: "cat" });
context.checkout.fail = true;
```

TypeScript ensures:
- property existence
- method existence
- argument shape correctness

TypeScript is used for **validation only**, not execution.

---

## Capability Model

The agent may only use capabilities that exist on `context`.

If a requested operation is not supported:

### Example

```
.agent make checkout fail
```

If `context.checkout.fail` does not exist:

**Response:**

```
Cannot complete request.
`context.checkout.fail` is not a supported property.

Suggested change:
Add a `fail` flag under `context.checkout` and update the route to return an error when enabled.
```

### Suggested Patch

```ts
export const POST: HTTP_POST = async ($) => {
  if ($.context.checkout?.fail) {
    return $.response[503].json({
      message: "Service unavailable",
    });
  }

  return $.response[200].random();
};
```

---

## Modes

### Default Mode (no preview)

- Executes immediately after validation
- Returns concise summary

### Debug Mode

```
.agent --debug add 10 cats
```

Shows:
- generated DSL
- validation results
- execution trace

### Patch Mode (implicit)

- Triggered when capability is missing
- Returns suggested code changes instead of executing

---

## Safety Guarantees

- No `eval`
- No arbitrary JavaScript execution
- DSL is parsed and interpreted directly
- Only `context` may be mutated
- Only declared methods/properties may be accessed
- Full validation occurs before execution

---

## Design Principles

- Explicit over implicit
- Capability-driven, not magic
- Interpreter over execution
- TypeScript for validation, not runtime
- DSL is the product, not JavaScript

---

## Implementation Plan (v1)

- [ ] Define DSL grammar (assignment + method call)
- [ ] Build DSL parser
- [ ] Normalize to internal operation format
- [ ] Generate TypeScript from DSL
- [ ] Integrate TypeScript type-checking
- [ ] Implement interpreter for operations
- [ ] Add `.agent` REPL command
- [ ] Add debug mode
- [ ] Add capability error + patch suggestion flow

---

## Future Enhancements

- Seeded randomness
- Rich helper utilities
- DSL compression (macros / repetition)
- Scenario libraries
- Replayable agent scripts
- UI for inspecting execution history

---

## Key Insight

The agent is not executing code.

It is generating a **deterministic sequence of context operations** that Counterfact validates and interprets.

This keeps the system safe, predictable, and aligned with how Counterfact already models state.

items.title: REPL-Native Request Builder with Autocomplete and OpenAPI Introspection
items.body:
## Summary

Introduce a REPL-first, fluent request builder that enables users to discover, construct, and execute API requests interactively.

This replaces the existing `client.*` interface with a more powerful abstraction:

> A **composable, introspectable request builder** designed for exploration.

The builder should:

- support fluent chaining
- allow partial application and reuse
- provide OpenAPI-backed autocomplete
- expose rich inline documentation
- guide users toward valid requests

---

## Core Idea

The request builder is the primary interface.

```js
const pet = route("/pet/{petId}/findByStatus")
  .method("get")
  .path({ petId: 1 });

await pet.query({ status: "sold" }).send();
```

This is not just a way to make requests.

It is a **stateful, composable representation of a request** that can be explored and refined in the REPL.

---

## Key Capabilities

### 1. Fluent Builder API

```js
const pet = route("/pet/{petId}/findByStatus")
  .method("get")
  .path({ petId: 1 });

const sold = pet.query({ status: "sold" });
const available = pet.query({ status: "available" });

await sold.send();
await available.send();
await sold.path({ petId: 2 }).send();
```

### Properties

- Immutable (each step returns a new builder)
- Supports branching and reuse
- Designed for REPL workflows

---

## 2. Progressive Execution

Requests are **progressively executable**.

```js
await pet.send()
```

If required parameters are missing:

- Do NOT execute
- Provide actionable feedback

Example:

```
Cannot execute request.

Missing required parameters:
  path:
    - petId (number)

Optional:
  query:
    - status (available | pending | sold)
```

---

## 3. OpenAPI-Backed Introspection

Builders expose full OpenAPI metadata.

```js
pet.help()
```

### Example Output

```
GET /pet/{petId}/findByStatus

Description:
  Find pets by status for a given pet ID.

Path Parameters:
  petId (number, required)
    Description: ID of the pet

Query Parameters:
  status (string, optional)
    Allowed values: available | pending | sold
    Description: Status values to filter by

Headers:
  Authorization (string, optional)
    Description: API key

Responses:
  200 OK
    Description: Successful response
```

---

## 4. Builder Introspection API

```js
pet.ready()      // boolean
pet.missing()    // structured list
pet.help()       // rich documentation
```

---

## 5. REPL Display

Evaluating a builder directly:

```js
pet
```

Displays:

```
GET /pet/{petId}/findByStatus

Path:
  petId: [missing]

Query:
  status: [optional]

Ready: false
```

This makes the REPL self-documenting.

---

## 6. Autocomplete

Autocomplete should be powered by OpenAPI and the route registry.

### Route Selection

Typing:

```
route("/p
```

Suggests:

```
route("/pet/{petId}/findByStatus")
route("/pet")
```

### Heuristics

Prefer runnable suggestions:

```
route("/pet/0")                // preferred
route("/pet/{petId}")         // fallback
```

Rules:

- number → `0` or `1`
- enum → first value
- boolean → `true`
- string → example if available

---

### Builder Steps

After selecting a route:

- `.method("get")` → suggest valid HTTP methods
- `.path({ ... })` → suggest path parameter names
- `.query({ ... })` → suggest query parameter names
- `.headers({ ... })` → suggest header names

---

## 7. Design Principles

- The builder is the primary abstraction
- The REPL is the primary environment
- Execution (`.send()`) is separate from introspection
- Do not overload return types
- Prefer immutability
- Prefer real object shapes over dynamic/proxy magic
- Surface OpenAPI information at the point of use

---

## Big Picture

This is not just an API client.

This is a:

> **REPL-native API exploration system**

The request builder should allow users to:

- discover available routes
- understand them via OpenAPI metadata
- construct valid requests incrementally
- reuse and refine requests
- explore APIs interactively

---

## Migration Note

The existing `client.*` interface will be deprecated in favor of the request builder.

All new functionality should be built around `route(...)`.

items.title: Add route autocomplete to REPL for client.<method>("...")
items.body:
## Summary

Enhance the Counterfact REPL to support autocomplete for API routes when using the `client` helper.

When a user types:

```ts
client.get("
```

and presses Tab, the REPL should suggest available routes derived from the route registry.

This improves discoverability and makes the REPL feel like an interactive API explorer.

## Problem

Currently, the REPL only supports basic Node.js tab completion based on runtime objects.

It does not support:
- autocompleting string arguments
- suggesting valid API routes
- helping users discover available endpoints

This makes the REPL less useful, especially for new users who do not know the available routes.

## Expected Behavior

When typing in the REPL:

```ts
client.get("/p
```

Pressing Tab should suggest matching routes such as:

```ts
"/pets"
"/pets/{petId}"
```

This should work for all HTTP methods:

- `client.get(...)`
- `client.post(...)`
- `client.put(...)`
- `client.patch(...)`
- `client.delete(...)`

## Implementation Approach

Use the `completer` option from Node's `repl` module.

Reference:
https://nodejs.org/api/repl.html#replstartoptions

### Step 1: Inject the registry into `startRepl`

Update the `startRepl()` signature so it receives the registry object.

It currently receives `contextRegistry`, `config`, and `print`.

It should also receive `registry`, since the paths live under `registry.routes`.

Example:

```ts
startRepl(contextRegistry, registry, config, print)
```

### Step 2: Add a completer

Update `repl.start()` in `startRepl()`:

```ts
const replServer = repl.start({
  prompt: "⬣> ",
  completer: createCompleter(registry),
});
```

### Step 3: Implement `createCompleter`

Create a function that:

1. Detects when the user is typing inside:
   - `client.get("...`
   - `client.post("...`
   - `client.put("...`
   - `client.patch("...`
   - `client.delete("...`

2. Extracts the partially typed route

3. Reads all available paths from `registry.routes`

4. Returns matching routes

Example:

```ts
function createCompleter(registry: Registry) {
  const routes = Object.keys(registry.routes);

  return (line: string) => {
    const match = line.match(
      /client\.(get|post|put|patch|delete)\("([^"]*)$/u,
    );

    if (!match) {
      return [[], line];
    }

    const partial = match[2];

    const matches = routes.filter((route) => route.startsWith(partial));

    return [matches, partial];
  };
}
```

### Step 4: Preserve existing REPL behavior

Make sure this does not break:
- `.proxy`
- `.counterfact`
- existing object/property completion where possible

If the current input does not match a supported `client.<method>("...")` pattern, the REPL should fall back cleanly.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Typing `client.get("` and pressing Tab shows route suggestions
- Partial matches filter correctly using prefix matching
- Works for:
  - `client.get(...)`
  - `client.post(...)`
  - `client.put(...)`
  - `client.patch(...)`
  - `client.delete(...)`
- Uses `registry.routes` as the source of truth
- `startRepl()` is updated to accept the registry object
- Existing REPL commands still work
- Non-matching input does not break normal REPL behavior

items.title: Support Multiple API Versions
items.body:
Possibly related to #1572 . We have consumers of Counterfact that are supporting versioned APIs. Each version has its own Spec file but technically the same `basePath`. Actually OpenApi 3 does away with the `basePath` preferring the `servers` collection. So we can't rely on `basePath` to distinguish specs. Should we combine these two issues? Technically this one is slightly different in that we need to support multiple specs base on the version.

The problem is there isn't a single way to denote variant versions of a spec. Read this discussion here: 
https://www.userosetta.com/blog/simplify-api-versioning-with-openapi

There is the `info.version` field in the spec header, but the stated purpose of that field isn't specifically to version the APIs so much as to version changes to the document. However, our consumers use that very field to denote the `v1`, `v2`, `v3`, etc versions. And the above article suggests using that header field is a perfectly valid way to distinguish versions.

Let's discuss the best path to implement this. I think it is reasonable to use the `version` field, but do we also infer the version from the `servers` collection as some documentation suggests?

In any case, it seems that if we load multiple specs that are variants, we need to build the types indedepently so that even if each spec has the same component name for a model we store it in a versioned path so that each model variant exists to be available as a type. So a `v1` and `v2` set of specs might have a component named `PetModel` live in two potential import paths:

`/components/schemas/v1/PetModel`
`/components/schemas/v2/PetModel`

items.title: Add `$.cookie` helper for reading request cookies (type-safe, spec-aware)
items.body:
## Description

Implement a request helper for accessing cookies:

```ts
$.cookie(name)
```

This helper should provide a clean, type-safe way to read cookies from the incoming request without manually parsing the `Cookie` header.

This mirrors `$.user` (basic auth) and aligns with Counterfact’s goal of providing high-level, intention-based APIs instead of raw HTTP handling.

---

## Example usage

```ts
export const GET = async ($) => {
  const sessionId = $.cookie("sessionId");

  return $.response.json({ sessionId });
};
```

With optional fallback:

```ts
const theme = $.cookie("theme") ?? "light";
```

---

## Requirements

1. Add a `cookie(name)` method on the request context `$`.
2. The method must return:
   - `string | undefined` (undefined if cookie is not present)
3. Must correctly parse the `Cookie` header from the request.
4. Must handle multiple cookies in a single header.
5. Must be safe and not throw on malformed cookie headers.
6. Must not require users to manually access headers.

---

## Behavior details

- Parse the `Cookie` header according to standard format:
  - `"key1=value1; key2=value2"`
- Trim whitespace around keys and values.
- Return the decoded value (URL-decoding if applicable).
- If the cookie is not present, return `undefined`.
- If duplicate cookie names exist, return the first occurrence.

---

## Type safety (Phase 1)

Basic API:

```ts
cookie(name: string): string | undefined;
```

---

## Type safety (Phase 2 - spec-aware)

If the OpenAPI spec defines cookies using:

- `in: cookie` parameters
- or `apiKey` security schemes with `in: cookie`

then generate a union type of known cookie names:

```ts
type RequestCookieName = "sessionId" | "theme";
```

And narrow the API:

```ts
cookie(name: RequestCookieName): string | undefined;
```

Fallback to `string` if the spec is not specific enough.

---

## Implementation guidance

- Reuse existing request header access if available.
- Implement a small internal cookie parser (avoid heavy dependencies).
- Cache parsed cookies per request to avoid repeated parsing.
- Keep parsing logic isolated and testable.

---

## Suggested steps

1. Locate request context (`$`) implementation.
2. Add `cookie(name)` method.
3. Implement cookie parsing utility.
4. Cache parsed result on first access.
5. Add tests for:
   - single cookie
   - multiple cookies
   - missing cookie
   - malformed header
   - whitespace handling
   - URL-encoded values

---

## Acceptance criteria

- `$.cookie("a")` returns the correct value when present.
- Returns `undefined` when cookie is missing.
- Handles multiple cookies correctly.
- Does not throw on malformed input.
- Works alongside existing request helpers.
- Tests pass.

---

## Out of scope

- Setting cookies (`$.response.cookie()` is handled separately)
- Cookie signing or encryption
- Automatic auth/session handling
- OpenAPI response cookie support

---

## Implementation notes for Copilot

Make the smallest clean change that fits the current architecture.  
Prefer extending existing request context patterns.  
Cache parsed cookies for efficiency.  
Include tests.

items.title: Add chainable `$.response.cookie()` helper for setting response cooki
items.body:
## Description

Implement a new response helper:

```ts
$.response.cookie(name, value, options?)
```

This helper should allow route handlers to add one or more cookies to the response without manually building `Set-Cookie` header strings.

---

## Example usage

```ts
export const GET = async ($) => {
  return $.response
    .cookie("sessionId", "abc123", {
      httpOnly: true,
      secure: true,
      sameSite: "lax",
      path: "/",
      maxAge: 3600
    })
    .json({ ok: true });
};
```

Multiple cookies should work:

```ts
return $.response
  .cookie("sessionId", "abc123")
  .cookie("theme", "dark")
  .json({ ok: true });
```

---

## Requirements

1. Add a `cookie(name, value, options?)` method to the response builder.  
2. The method must be chainable and return the response builder instance.  
3. Each call must append a new `Set-Cookie` value rather than overwriting prior cookies.  
4. Cookie values must be serialized into valid `Set-Cookie` strings.  
5. This must integrate cleanly with the existing response-building flow.  
6. Do not require route authors to call `.header("Set-Cookie", ...)` manually.  

---

## Supported options

Support these option fields:

```ts
type CookieOptions = {
  domain?: string;
  expires?: Date;
  httpOnly?: boolean;
  maxAge?: number;
  path?: string;
  sameSite?: "lax" | "strict" | "none";
  secure?: boolean;
};
```

---

## Behavior details

- `name` and `value` should be strings.  
- `maxAge` should serialize as `Max-Age=<number>`.  
- `expires` should serialize as `Expires=<UTC string>`.  
- Boolean flags like `HttpOnly` and `Secure` should be included only when true.  
- `sameSite` should serialize as `SameSite=Lax`, `SameSite=Strict`, or `SameSite=None`.  
- `path` and `domain` should serialize normally when provided.  
- Preserve the order of cookie attributes in a consistent way.  
- Multiple cookies must survive all the way to the final HTTP response as distinct `Set-Cookie` values.  

---

## Implementation guidance

- Reuse existing response header infrastructure where practical.  
- If headers are currently stored as single values, update the implementation so `Set-Cookie` can support multiple values safely without breaking other headers.  
- Prefer a small internal serializer function over adding a large dependency.  
- Keep the change focused. Do not add cookie parsing or request-side cookie APIs in this issue.  

---

## Suggested steps

1. Find the response builder implementation.  
2. Add a `cookie()` method.  
3. Add a small internal cookie serialization utility.  
4. Ensure response headers can carry multiple `Set-Cookie` values.  
5. Add or update tests for:
   - one cookie  
   - multiple cookies  
   - all supported options  
   - chaining with existing response helpers like `.json()`  

---

## Acceptance criteria

- `$.response.cookie("a", "1")` adds one valid `Set-Cookie` header.  
- Multiple `.cookie()` calls produce multiple `Set-Cookie` header values.  
- `.cookie()` can be chained before or after `.json()`, `.example()`, or other response helpers.  
- Existing response behavior continues to work.  
- Tests pass.  

---

## Out of scope

- `$.cookies`  
- `clearCookie()`  
- OpenAPI cookie metadata  
- automatic auth or session features  

---

## Implementation notes for Copilot

Make the smallest clean change that fits the current architecture.  
Prefer extending existing response-builder patterns over introducing a parallel mechanism.  
Include tests.
Include documentation.
Include a changeset.

items.title: Invalid example name returns 200 “ok” instead of failing
items.body:
## Minimal repro

OpenAPI path:

```yaml 
/hello/{name}:
  get:
    parameters:
      - in: path
        name: name
        required: true
        schema:
          type: string
    responses:
      default:
        description: Successful response
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: string
            examples:
              hello-example1:
                value: Hello, example1
              hello-example2:
                value: Hello, example2
```

Route:

```ts
import type { HTTP_GET } from "../../types/paths/hello/{name}.types.js";

export const GET: HTTP_GET = async ($) => {
  return $.response[200].example("hello-example3");
};
```

Steps to reproduce

1. Define the OpenAPI path above.
2. Implement the route above.
3. Send GET /hello/whatever.

## Expected behavior

Counterfact should fail because hello-example3 does not exist.
A 500 error would be acceptable.

## Actual behavior

Counterfact returns:
- status: 200
- body: "ok"

## Notes

The route is requesting an example name that is not defined in the OpenAPI document.
Instead of surfacing that as an error, Counterfact appears to fall back to a successful default response.

It's probably due to a larger issue, that exceptions are swallowed somewhere.

items.title: Midleware matching all routes is not executed
Optional parameters are marked as required when they reference a schema with a required property containing list of sub properties
items.body:
Reference

For a OpenAPI spec like:

```yaml
openapi: 3.0.3
info:
  title: Minimal Reproduction
  version: 1.0.0
paths: {}
components:
  schemas:
    Example:
      type: object
      properties:
        requiredField:
          type: string
        optionalObjectWithRequiredSubField:
          type: object
          properties:
            subField:
              type: string
          required:
            - subField   # <-- this nested required array causes counterfact to
                         #     incorrectly mark optionalObjectWithRequiredSubField
                         #     as required at the parent level
      required:
        - requiredField  # optionalObjectWithRequiredSubField is intentionally absent
```

The expected generated TypeScript type would be:

```typescript
type Example = {
  requiredField: string;
  optionalObjectWithRequiredSubField?: { subField: string };  // should be optional
};
```

but the actual result is incorrect like so:

```typescript
type Example = {
  requiredField: string;
  optionalObjectWithRequiredSubField: { subField: string };  // incorrectly required
};
```

items.title: Raise error for schema name conflict
items.body:
In our use case we're merging multiple YAML files before using Counterfact to generate types from them. Occasionally two different files will have two schema with the same name, in which case Counterfact silently generates only one `.ts` file, presumably corresponding to whichever schema it processed second (i.e. the second overwrites the first).

This failure mode can be tricky to detect manually, as often the two schema are similar enough in shape that it doesn't immediately cause TS errors. It would be nice if Counterfact would warn us by raising an error (detectable in CI) when it encounters multiple schema with the same name.

items.body:
Hi,
I have a "weird" OpenAPI spec where they use colons in their paths to distinguish different endpoints, much like Wikipedia does (e.g. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talk:Main_Page). This is perfectly valid for URLs.

The issue with counterfact is that these paths cause the route file names to have the colons in them, which is perfectly fine on macOS/Linux, but not at all supported on Windows/NTFS. Git on macOS even warns me about that before commiting.

So I think this needs to be changed somehow, since there is no easy workaround I could think of apart from editing that OpenAPI spec file, which is not something I should be forced to do.

items.title: MaybeShortcut for content type is too strict
items.body:
Openapi library, which I am using, uses `application/json; charset=utf-8` for json responses as content type. Current `MaybeShortcut` implementation expects exact match of content type which make json field not available. My suggestion is to use contains instead of exact content match. Like so:
```ts
type IfHasKey<
  SomeObject,
  Keys extends readonly string[],
  Yes,
  No,
> = Keys extends [infer FirstKey, ...infer RestKeys]
  ? Extract<
      keyof SomeObject,
      `${string}${FirstKey & string}${string}`
    > extends never
    ? IfHasKey<SomeObject, RestKeys & readonly string[], Yes, No>
    : Yes
  : No;
```
