items.title: Add Warning to Module Tree if Ambiguous Wildcards Detected
items.body: While it is invalid API spec to have two wildcard paths at the same path defined (see issue #1308) it is possible to end up in a state where you have two such as the referenced issue or from just manually creating a second endpoint. The `module-tree.ts` class has enough logic in place to be aware that more than a single leaf wildcard path has been found for a given path. We should at the least show a console log warning when this is detected to raise awareness to the consumer.

items.title: Add Prune option for clearing out defunct paths and endpoints
items.body:
Sometimes an OpenApi spec might change path names or endpoint names. In that case, if a consumer tries to run Counterfact again, since it will leave the old paths and routes alone it is possible to end up with multiple wild card routes at the same end path. Example:

Old path:
`/pet/{id}/update/{Name}.ts`
New path:
`/pet/{id}/update/{nickname}.ts`

In this case, the old file will be left in place and the new one created. Then when `module-tree.ts` attempts to resolve the path it will have ambiguity because both wildcards can be a math if they both have the same HTTP verb.

We should offer a `--prune` option that will clean out any paths that aren't represented in the OpenApi spec.

items.title: Add startup option for building the cache
items.body: The current implementation only transpiles the routes and contexts when you start the server. The transpiler presently only runs in the `start()` function returned by the `counterfact` function and only when the `startServer` option is true. We should have a CLI option to transpile the code to cache without running the server so that test environments can buid the cache as part of the test harness startup. This will be necessary for the new MSW functionality because without it the user has to be sure they have started CF at least once.

items.title: Quickstart command out of date
items.body:
[Quickstart](https://counterfact.dev/docs/quick-start.html) suggests the following command:

```sh
npx counterfact@latest https://petstore3.swagger.io/api/v3/openapi.json api --open
```

This doesn't seem to match the syntax provided by `--help` which indicates options should go between the command and the schema location:

```sh
Usage: counterfact [options] [openapi.yaml] [destination]
```

I thought this might be why the server wasn't starting, but moving the option flag alone didn't fix it. The server still wasn't started, I'm returned immediately to my shell, and the opened browser naturally can't connect. Using debug output, I determined `generate` is set to `{ routes: undefined, types: undefined }` when `--open` is used. Adding `-g` as an option alongside `--open` does result in the expected route and type generation, but the server still stops immediately after being started and I'm returned to a shell. I had to additionally add `-s` as an option to keep the server running and for the browser opened by `--open` to correctly load the Swagger UI.

items.title: Middleware (formerly "interceptors")
items.body:
There ought to be a way to add behavior that applies to all routes or all routes within a directory. This will be useful for use cases like handling authentication globally. 

I'm thinking about adding an extension point via an _.intercept.ts file. 

The file would export a function that looks like this:

```ts
export const intercept: INTERCEPT = ($, respondTo, path, method) => {
  return respondTo($);
}
```

The respondTo function is the operation function (GET, POST, etc) in the file corresponding to the path. The idea here is we can modify the request before it's passed to that function and modify the response after it's returned from the function. We can also skip the function altogether and return a different response. 

It's basically a middleware but I hesitate to call it that because relating it to express / koa middleware may cause confusion. 

Type safety may be a bit involved here. That INTERCEPT type will have to be overloaded with a type for each combination of path and method. The argument and return type of `respondTo` can be imported from files that specify path types.

items.title: Better explanation of why generated code should be committed to version control
items.body:
Is there any good reason to commit generated code for types to version control? In the documentation I wrote that those files should be committed, but now I can't remember what my reasoning was. 

If the types code isn't committed, I think that would alleviate confusion when a new version of Counterfact generates types differently from the previous version. 

Counterfact creates a `.gitignore` file for the `.cache` directory and that seems to work fine. I can't think of a reason we shouldn't add the types directories to that file.

items.title: Put all generated types under a "types" directory
items.body:
A fairly simple change:

- `path-types` -> `types/paths`
- `components` -> `types/components`
- `paths` -> `routes`

I think it will be easier to understand what's what. The structure of the types directory should resemble the structure of the OpenAPI spec. And "routes" is a clearer indicator of what the directory contains. 

I don't like to catch people off guard with disruptive changes like this. If we're going to do it, it should be before 1.0.

        - message
```

According to [Reusing Responses](https://swagger.io/docs/specification/describing-responses/), I should be able to extract common schemas under `components/responses` like so:

```yaml
paths:

  /path-one:
      responses:
        "400":
          $ref: "#/components/responses/BadRequest"

components:

  responses:

    BadRequest:
      description: The request is malformed and so cannot be processed
      content:
        application/json:
          schema:
            $ref: '#/components/schemas/Error'

  schemas:

    Error:
      title: Error
      description: A generic error message suitable for 4xx and 5xx responses
      type: object
      properties:
        code:
          type: string
          description: A machine readable error code
        message:
          type: string
          description: A detailed description of the error
      required:
        - message
```

However, with that configuration I have a few problems.

First, no `Error.ts` type is generated.

Second, the `*.types.ts` file is missing expected types. Specifically, the `content` has `never` type:

```ts
export type HTTP_POST = (
  $: OmitValueWhenNever<{
[...]
    response: ResponseBuilderFactory<{
      400: {
        headers: never;
        requiredHeaders: never;
        content: never;
      };
```

whereas previously it was correct:

```ts
      400: {
        headers: never;
        requiredHeaders: never;
        content: {
          "application/json": {
            schema: Error;
          };
        };
      };
```

Note this isn't strictly a blocker to using counterfact (for me) as I can avoid the refactoring and keep the duplication to get counterfact to do the right thing. However, for others who may not be in control how the spec is written, this could be a problem.

If I may speculate on the root cause, I presume this is because counterfact has its own bespoke OpenAPI parser? If so, a quick search has found tools like https://www.npmjs.com/package/@readme/openapi-parser which may provide a complete parser that handles all the `$ref`s and other subtleties of the OpenAPI spec. I only point this out as this specific issue may be fixed, but it does give me pause as to what other issues I may encounter using counterfact with specs that use lesser-known parts of OpenAPI. Of course, switching out parsers is likely a non-trivial amount of work.

items.title: Hot reloading does not reload all files
items.body:
(Created from #823)

While hot reloading will reload a changed file, it does not appear that changes are actually used. For example, a changed file in the `paths/` directory will be reloaded. However, those changes have no effect until the `_.context.ts` file is reloaded as well.

## Steps to reproduce
### Setup
Have a file structure like so:
```
counterfact/
    paths/
        _mocks/
            my-custom-code.ts
        _.context.ts
```

In `_.context.ts`:
```ts
import { CustomClass } from './_mocks/my-custom-code';

console.log("_.context.ts loaded");
// Do stuff with CustomClass
```

In `./_mocks/my-custom-code`:

```ts
console.log("Custom code loaded");

const value = "Some value that's used in generating a mock response";

class CustomClass {
  // Use value in here somehow as part of generating a response
}

export { CustomClass }
```
### Trigger

1. Run counterfact (ex: `npx counterfact spec.openapi.yaml counterfact`)
2. Call counterfact api, see the `"Some value..."` in the HTTP response
3. Modify the custom code string to be something else (`"const value = "Changed!"`)
4. Note that `Custom code loaded` is logged
5. Make a request to counterfact. Note that the new value is not returned

However, if I trivially modify the `_.context.ts` file (touch it, add a comment, etc), I do see counterfact log the `_.context.ts loaded` message. If I then make a new HTTP request, I see the new value in the mock http response.

items.title: Ability to run Counterfact without OpenAPI
items.body:
Counterfact works fine without an OpenAPI description. It just won't generate code for you. You have to create JavaScript* files manually under the `paths` directory. The easiest way to implement is to supply an empty OpenAPI object if no file is given. In the CLI, a `-` can stand for the empty OpenAPI object.

```sh
npx counterfact - ./api 
```

The `-` could become the default value for the OpenAPI file path argument. If you're happy for files to be in the default location (the current working directory), it could be run with no arguments at all.

```sh
npx counterfact
```


----

*Either JavaScript or TypeScript would work, but TypeScript without the automatically generated types would not be fun.

items.title: Toggle proxy for individual endpoints
items.body:
The `.proxy [on|off]` command enables the proxy to be enabled or disabled at runtime. 

At times, it's useful to be able to turn the proxy on only for particular endpoints. One way to do that now is to use the `$.proxy()` function. But it would be nice to have the option to toggle in the CLI (and eventually also the GUI) without changing code:

items.title: Add CLI option to skip generating types
items.body:
Every time Counterfact is launched it generates all the various `.types` files and paths based on the OpenApi doc. It would be nice if there were an option for the command line to skip generating the files (and basically just tell CF to assume all the types and components are already generated). I realize we need CF to generate the types and such, but lately we have seen that when a version bump happens for CF with a new feature it updates all the generated types. Our users are often caught off guard by this and don't know if they should commit these types or not when they aren't really intending to change anything with our mocks. 

Our plan is to explicitly generate the types and components only when we know the OpenApi spec has been updated. We do realize this means a new feature to CF that might need a re-gen of the types and models would be skipped, but it would allow us to have more control over when those types get updated and committed.

items.title: Support for basic auth
items.body:
Counterfact doesn't currently read [the security object of the OpenAPI schema](https://swagger.io/specification/#oas-security). 

When generating types, it should take that object into account. 

For example, if the security object is defined as:

```json
{
  "type": "http",
  "scheme": "basic"
}
```

Then Counterfact should read the username and add it to a `$.user` object. 

Note: this only covers "http" authentication. OpenAPI also "apiKey", "mutualTLS", "oauth2", "openIdConnect". Eventually we'll want to support "apiKey" and "oauth2" as well. I'm not sure the others worth pursuing.

items.title: Support for API key
items.body:
Counterfact doesn't currently read [the security object of the OpenAPI schema](https://swagger.io/specification/#oas-security). 

When generating types, it should take that object into account. 

For example, if the security object is defined as:

```json
{
  "type": "apiKey",
  "name": "api_key",
  "in": "header"
}
```

Then Counterfact should act as if every operation has a required request header named "api_key" when generating code. 

Note: this only covers "apiKey" authentication. OpenAPI also "http", "mutualTLS", "oauth2", "openIdConnect". Eventually we'll want to support "http" and "oauth2" as well. I'm not sure the others worth pursuing.

items.title: further isolate black box tests
items.body:
I've had a couple of issues where the code passed all of the tests but did not work when installed via npx. 

The [black box tests](https://github.com/pmcelhaney/counterfact/blob/main/test/black-box.test.js) should create a "release" and then install / run it using npx. 

1. use `npm pack` to create tarball (`.tgz`) file
2. use [pacote](https://www.npmjs.com/package/pacote#extract) (the same library npm uses under the hood) to extract the `.tgz` file to a directory, e.g. `release-candidate`
3. Run the cli using `npx ./release-candidate` 

That way the test suite will truly be black box tests, in a clean environment with no dependencies on source code.

items.title: hot reloading doesn't work outside a package with type:module
items.body:
Counterfact transpiles TypeScript files to JS and puts them in a folder called `.cache`. Those files are `import()`ed with a query string at the end of the URL to bust the cache. The cache busing mechanism doesn't work if the files are CJS.

To ensure the files are modules, we used the `.mjs` extension on transpiled files. That worked great until I wanted to import another file from my `_.context.ts` file. The import didn't work because it was trying to import a `.js` file instead of a `.mjs` file. I could probably mess around with the TypeScript settings to make it work, but that felt clunky.

So I went back to transpiling to `.js` files and looked for a package.json to determine whether those files should be modules or CommonJS. That worked great except for the fact that hot reloading doesn't work in CommonJS.

A few possible ways to solve this problem:

1. Add a package.json to the .cache directory. The downside is if you want the generated code to be inside an existing package, it will create a new package which is not desirable. We could mitigate by creating the package.json if and only if there isn't already a package.json higher up with `"type": "module"`. That would work unless someone wants to use Counterfact inside a CommonJS module. At this point, I'm not particularly concerned about supporting that use case. 

2. Load modules using a VM. This might be the simplest and best option. Since you pass code to a VM instead of a file name, we can be sure that caching is not an issue. We can also ensure that files that are imported / required are not cached. A whole other problem that other solutions don't address.

3. Go back to `.mjs` files.

4. <del>Use `module.require()` instead of `import()` and manually manage Node's cache?</del> that doesn't work  


Okay, now that I've written that out I think option 2 is going to make the most sense, with option 1 as a stopgap. I did a little bit of testing and it looks like we can use vm.Script() even when loading modules. We don't need to use the experimental VM modules. For CJS we can pass a modified version of `require()` to the context that busts cache. I'm not sure how `import()` would work but I guess it's a similar idea.

items.title: A changed property in the context file does not get picked up immediately
Import the nearest _.context.ts
items.body:
A file under `path-types` imports a file called `_.context.ts`

Currently that imported file is in the parallel directory under `paths`, e.g. `/paths-types/foo/bar` imports `paths/foo/bar/_.context.ts`.

But what if there is no `paths/foo/bar/_.context.ts` file? In that case it should import `paths/foo/_.context.ts`, or `paths/_.context.ts`, i.e. the the nearest file found when walking up the directory.

> [!NOTE]
> The way the code works currently, every directory has a `_.context.ts`, which by default exports its parent (`export { Context } from "../_.context.ts";`). That's a kludge and the current implementation has a bug: if there are no endpoints under a particular path, the file won't be created.

items.title: Command/Context API to Let External Concerns Manipulate Counterfact

Presently we can use the REPL to work with a specific context and toggle various settings, alter data, etc, while running our UI against the mock server so we can test various alternating scenarios. Think of an authentication endpoint that might have 3 or 4 different response types (invalid password, password change required, etc).

Ideally we could have a set of API calls to the Counterfact server that have nothing to do with the Open API spec, but are specific to controlling Counterfact. In a Playwright test I could have a UI test that exercises all the various paths of an auth scenario (see above) without having to "bake" into the mock logic special hardcoded values such as different usernames that exercise the various response paths. Instead we could just have our mock context expose functions that let us easily toggle back and forth between the various response states. Our E2E test could run a set of test, then hit the Counterfact command API to switch the response state, rerun the tests and have it exercise the other paths.

items.title: root context isn't reused
items.body:
The context object defined in `paths/$.context.ts` is supposed to be shared across all paths by default. Users are able to create more localized contexts, by, for example, creating a `/paths/a/$.context.ts` file for all paths under `/paths/a`.

The code under `/path-types` needs a reference to the _type_ of the Context object for that path. So I cleverly created a default `$.context.ts` that is simply `export default from "../$.context";`. 

So in theory, each path has its own context, but all contexts by default are aliases to the root context. In practice that's not how it works because imports are cache busted, so every time a context module is loaded, the module is executed again and a new instance of `Context` is generated (because `new Context()` is run again). 

To fix it, the `contextRegistry` needs to not store a new context object for a path unless it really does have its own distinct context object.

I think I can make this happen by changing `export default from "../$.context";` to `export type ContextType from "../$.context";` And make sure if the default export is undefined, it doesn't get placed in the `contextRegistry`. 

The root context will have `export type ContextType = typeof ContextType`. 

The path-types files will import `ContextType` instead of the default export. In the path-types files `typeof Context` will also change to `ContextType`.

Will this be a breaking change? Files in `path-types` get regenerated every time so they're okay. The `$.context.ts` files would need to be deleted and regenerated. Unless they were manually modified. Then they will need to have an `export type ContextType = typeof Context;` added at the end. I guess I could use JSCodeShift to preprocess and migrate those files.

items.title: Rewrite the TypeScript generator

labels.name: archive
labels.description: Mostly Patrick brainstorming in the early days

items.body:
I'd like to convert the TypeScript generator code from JavaScript to TypeScript, but I keep running into a wall with the Requirement class. A Requirement is a wrapper for a node in the OpenAPI spec. 

## Option 1: Fix the Requirement Class

The Requirement class has three parts:

- the data (the node itself)
- a reference to the specification
- a URL (where it is in relation to the specification)

A few methods assume the data is an object, which is making adding type annotations difficult. It might help if we split the Requirement class into `BranchRequirement` and `LeafRequirement`. (Note that when the data is an array, it's treated as an object with numeric keys.) 

## Option 2: Rewrite the whole thing

This was originally written as a proof of concept. I wasn't sure where I was going with it, or if I could even pull it off. Now that I know what I want to achieve, it might make sense to take a step back and rewrite the whole thing from scratch.

## Option 3: Do nothing

The code works and it's not terribly difficult to modify to add new features. So maybe it's best to leave the code in JavaScript for now.

milestone.title: Version 1.0
milestone.description:
This project will reach 1.0 when mutation test coverage is > 90% and:

The following command

```sh
npx counterfact init ./my-petstore https://petstore3.swagger.io/api/v3/openapi.yaml
```

creates or augments an npm package, and after changing to the directory

```sh
cd my-petstore
```

the following command

```sh
yarn start

```

opens a browser with Swagger-UI pointing to a server that implements the pet store API.

Not a mock server that returns canned or randomly generated responses, a real implementation, written in TypeScript.

Or at least, the potential for a real implementation. Out of the box, it will return example or random responses. But the code is easy to edit so, e.g., we can change PUT /pet to store a Pet in memory / a database / a microservice / etc., and GET /pet to retrieve that same Pet.

We can see the effects of the code changes without restarting the server.

And then after running

```sh
npm run counterfact generate /path/to/copy/of/petstore/with/some/changes.yaml
```

it regenerates the code except for the files that we changed. Of the files we changed, the IDE (via TypeScript and ESLint) tells us if the code needs to be modified to conform to the updated spec.

Again, without restarting the server.


---- 

Update 2913-09-06

All of the above is done except 90% test coverage (which is close). In fact, it works a lot better than what I wrote above. There are a few little tweaks I would like to add before stamping 1.0 and spreading the word. 


## GUI (web page)

Add a field to enter the proxy address, and a checkbox / toggle to turn it on and off globally.

Put the list of paths in a table and add columns for:

- proxy (checkbox or toggle)
- methods (one or multiple columns with icons representing the standard HTTP methods)
  - could link directly to the implementations for each method in the IDE

Use a websocket to keep the above information current.

Put a REPL in the GUI.

## Config file

`.counterfact.yaml` can have the path to the OpenAPI spec, the proxy URL, whether the proxy is on (globally), and whether the proxy is on for individual paths

An "extends" field so we can have a base config which is committed to the repo and a local config which is in `.gitignore`

## Code generation

Use the OpenAPI spec to generate JSDocs.

Move `paths-js` to `.cache` to make it clear these files aren't meant to be edited.

Import models that will likely be useful. (https://github.com/pmcelhaney/counterfact/issues/529)

## Watch the OpenAPI file

If the OpenAPI file is local, watch it for changes and regenerate code.

## TypeScript

While Counterfact generates TypeScript, Counterfact itself was originally written in JavaScript. The server code is now in TypeScript. Now just need to update the typescript-generator code.

## REPL

Finalize the API for `.proxy`: `.proxy [on|off [path]]`, `.proxy set url`

## Server

### Add the Open API document to $

The particular use case I have in mind is being able to pass a schema to json-schema-faker, so that we can exercise fine-grained control over what is generated.

```ts
export const GET: HTTP_GET = ($) => {
  const randomPet = jsf.generate($.openapi.components.schemas.Pet.schema);
  return $.response[200].json(randomPet);
};
```

milestone.description: Future enhancements that are not (yet) tied to any upcoming release

items.body:
[Talkback](https://github.com/ijpiantanida/talkback) is a library which forwards HTTP requests to a proxy, records the responses, and replays them later.

Rather than reinvent the wheel, Counterfact could integrate with talkback. When proxy mode is on, a developer can also turn talkback mode on, change out the "tapes", and adjust other talkback related settings, through CLI arguments, the GUI, or the REPL.


Probably a better idea than #451

items.title: VCR type functionality
$.proxy() incorrectly calls fetch()
items.body:
Not sure what I was thinking when I wrote this:

```js
        const fetchResponse = await this.fetch(options.host, {
          method,
          path,
          headers: new Headers(headers),
          query,
          ...options,
        });
```

`path` and `query` should be part of the URL (the first argument). They should not be in the options. And I'm not sure what I intended to do with `...options`. 

In `koa-middleware.js`, the call to `dispatcher.request` should pass `ctx.req` (the underlying Node request object). The URL should be then be `${host}${req.path}` (`req.path` includes the query string).

items.title: Elevator pitch
items.body:
Brainstorming. Thinking about putting this in the README. 

| |Counterfact|Your Production Back End|
|-|-|-|
|To front end code it's...|a fully functional REST API|a fully functional REST API|
|Secure, scalable, robust, etc.|doesn't need to be| yes (🤞) |
|Cost to build|$|$$$$$|
|Implementing a typical feature<sup>1</sup> takes|minutes|days? weeks?|
|Can be gradually replaced with production code| yes | n/a |
|Running locally requires|node| probably a lot more than that |
|See code changes|when you hit save | after compile + restart / deploy |
|Change behavior without losing server-side state| yes (hot reload) | wait, what?|
|Play with the state in a REPL | yes | not likely |
|Maintainable by front end devs | yes | maybe?|
|Reproducing weird stuff that happened in prod | easy | hard / impossible |
|API response time|negligible|varies|
|Maintaining test accounts is | optional | required |
|Integrates with UI tests (Jest, Playwright, etc.)| [coming soon] |no|
|Seed with test data / scenarios| [coming soon] | much slower if possible at all |
|Optimized for | developers | end users |
|Developer experience | 😁 | 😣 |


<sup>1</sup> a change big enough to call out in release notes

items.body:
Support proxying to another server instead of using mocks. In addition to supporting the ability to proxy to another server, there are five different interfaces through which we may turn the proxy on or off.

## CLI
- [x] `--proxy-url [url]` to set the proxy URL

## Code
- [ ] `return $.proxy();` to use the proxy for an operation -- if no proxy is set return 502
- [x] `return $.proxy('https://example.com/specific-url');` to use the proxy via a specific URL

## REPL
- [x] `.proxy` to toggle the proxy globally
- [x] #440


## REST
To support the GUI

- [ ] `POST /counterfact/proxy/{url}` with the URL in the body to set the proxy URL
- [ ] `POST /counterfact/proxy` with `true` or `false` in the body to enable disable the proxy globally
- [ ] `GET /counterfact/proxy` to list individual operations and whether they're proxid 
- [ ] `POST /counterfact/proxy/operations` with an `{ path, method, isEnabled }[]` to toggle the proxy for individual URLs



## GUI
- [ ] a toggle to turn the proxy on and off
- [ ] an input to set the proxy URL
- [ ] individual toggles for each route

items.body:
See https://swagger.io/docs/specification/data-models/oneof-anyof-allof-not/

It should work just like https://github.com/bcherny/json-schema-to-typescript

In fact, I would love to use json-schema-to-typescript rather than rolling our own code. We need to augment that library with the ability to add our own $RefParser so that it can reference a type defined in another file.

items.title: When adding a server URL, add the full URL
items.body: Counterfact includes Swagger-UI. I loads the OpenAPI document through a proxy which puts itself at the top of the `servers` list in the OpenAPI document. Currently the URL it adds is just "/".  If the OpenAPI document has an entry for host, it will try to load `/` on the host instead of the localhost. To fix that, we need to change the "/" to "http://localhost:${port}/".

items.title: $context.js files aren't generated for in-between directories
items.body: Say an OpenAPI spec defines `/foo/bar/baz` and no other paths. When Counterfact generates`/foo/bar/$context.ts` it creates `/foo/bar/baz.ts` which references `/foo/$context.ts`. But since it's not generating any `/foo/*.ts` files it won't create the `/foo/$context.ts` file.

items.title: Non-alphanumeric characters in the component name break the code generator.
items.body:
To reproduce:

```sh
yarn counterfact https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stripe/openapi/master/openapi/spec3.yaml stripe
```

It results in an error. 

```
SyntaxError: ',' expected. (4:19)
  2 | import type { HttpStatusCode } from "counterfact";
  3 | import Context from "./../../../paths/v1/apps/$context.js";
> 4 | import type { apps.secret } from "./../../../components/apps.secret.js";
    |                   ^
```

There's a component (under schemas) named `apps.secret`. That's not a valid variable name so we need to transform it to something like `apps_secret`.

items.body:
`response[statusCode].random()` uses JSONSchemaFaker to generate a random response. As long as the schema for the response is inline it works. It needs to be extended to work when the response is at a `$ref`. We need to either resolve all the references before calling JSONSchemaFaker or use it's `resolve()` method.

We need to trace the references at build time so we can generate TypeScript with a file structure that matches the structure at the document. At runtime, when we're using the document to generate random data, we don't care about where the data came from. We just want a simple JSON object.

items.body:
Code like this

```ts
      const property = this.requirement.select(`properties/${name}`);
```

Can be rewritten as

```ts
      const property = this.requirement.select("properties").select(name);
```

If we change `select()` so that it only takes one step, then we escape the "/" in a value. So code like this:

```ts
        const schema = responses
          .select(type.responseCode)
          .select("content")
          ?.select(type.contentType.replace("/", "~1"))
          ?.select("schema");
```

Becomes this:

```ts
        const schema = responses
          .select(type.responseCode)
          .select("content")
          ?.select(type.contentType)
          ?.select("schema");
```

```yaml

items.title: hot reload doesn't work in some cases
items.body:
1. run `yarn start demo` 
2. open http://localhost:3100/hello/world
3. make a change to `./demo/hello/{name}.js` 
4. reload  http://localhost:3100/hello/world

The change made in step 3 should be reflected. 

It's not because of this line in module-loader.js

```js
        const url = `/${nodePath.join(parts.dir, parts.name)}`;
```

The path already starts with a `/` so the URL ends up starting with `//`. 

I think it depends on whether `parts.dir` ends with a `/`.

milestone.title: Version 1.0
milestone.description:
This project will reach 1.0 when mutation test coverage is > 90% and:

The following command

```sh
npx counterfact init ./my-petstore https://petstore3.swagger.io/api/v3/openapi.yaml
```

creates or augments an npm package, and after changing to the directory

```sh
cd my-petstore
```

the following command

```sh
yarn start

```

opens a browser with Swagger-UI pointing to a server that implements the pet store API.

Not a mock server that returns canned or randomly generated responses, a real implementation, written in TypeScript.

Or at least, the potential for a real implementation. Out of the box, it will return example or random responses. But the code is easy to edit so, e.g., we can change PUT /pet to store a Pet in memory / a database / a microservice / etc., and GET /pet to retrieve that same Pet.

We can see the effects of the code changes without restarting the server.

And then after running

```sh
npm run counterfact generate /path/to/copy/of/petstore/with/some/changes.yaml
```

it regenerates the code except for the files that we changed. Of the files we changed, the IDE (via TypeScript and ESLint) tells us if the code needs to be modified to conform to the updated spec.

Again, without restarting the server.


---- 

Update 2913-09-06

All of the above is done except 90% test coverage (which is close). In fact, it works a lot better than what I wrote above. There are a few little tweaks I would like to add before stamping 1.0 and spreading the word. 


## GUI (web page)

Add a field to enter the proxy address, and a checkbox / toggle to turn it on and off globally.

Put the list of paths in a table and add columns for:

- proxy (checkbox or toggle)
- methods (one or multiple columns with icons representing the standard HTTP methods)
  - could link directly to the implementations for each method in the IDE

Use a websocket to keep the above information current.

Put a REPL in the GUI.

## Config file

`.counterfact.yaml` can have the path to the OpenAPI spec, the proxy URL, whether the proxy is on (globally), and whether the proxy is on for individual paths

An "extends" field so we can have a base config which is committed to the repo and a local config which is in `.gitignore`

## Code generation

Use the OpenAPI spec to generate JSDocs.

Move `paths-js` to `.cache` to make it clear these files aren't meant to be edited.

Import models that will likely be useful. (https://github.com/pmcelhaney/counterfact/issues/529)

## Watch the OpenAPI file

If the OpenAPI file is local, watch it for changes and regenerate code.

## TypeScript

While Counterfact generates TypeScript, Counterfact itself was originally written in JavaScript. The server code is now in TypeScript. Now just need to update the typescript-generator code.

## REPL

Finalize the API for `.proxy`: `.proxy [on|off [path]]`, `.proxy set url`

## Server

### Add the Open API document to $

The particular use case I have in mind is being able to pass a schema to json-schema-faker, so that we can exercise fine-grained control over what is generated.

```ts
export const GET: HTTP_GET = ($) => {
  const randomPet = jsf.generate($.openapi.components.schemas.Pet.schema);
  return $.response[200].json(randomPet);
};
```

items.body:
Building on #133

`response[statusCode].random()` returns a valid, randomly generated response, based on the schema provided by an OpenAPI document. 

For now, `response[statusCode].header('x-header', 'whatever').json('whatever').random()` ignores the header and content that were provided and provides a completely random value. In the future we'll want to keep whatever was provided and only randomize the parts that were not specified. In the future we'll want to keep whatever is provided and only randomize the remainder. 

In order for `random()` to work we need to provide Counterfact the OpenAPI document at runtime. It can be passed into the constructor. If Counterfact doesn't have an OpenAPI spec, return a 500 error with an explanation. 

This issue does not include type checking. That's covered in #136

items.body:
Handle multiple response types in the same return statement (without if (accepts(...)))). 

Currently the return type of a verb function looks like this:

```ts
type returnType = {
   status: HttpStatusCode,
   contentType: `${string}/${string}",
   headers: Record<string, string | number>,
   body: unknown
}
```

We need a way to handle a scenario where the API can return two or more different content types depending on what the client accepts.

```ts
type returnType = {
   status: HttpStatusCode,
   headers: Record<string, string | number>,
  content: { 
          media: `${string}/${string}",
          body: unknown
      }[],
}
```

In this case, the server will loop through each item in the content array and return the content-type + body of the first one that matches. If there are no matches it will return a 415 status code (or whatever code is most appropriate, need to double check that).

milestone.description: Future enhancements that are not (yet) tied to any upcoming release

items.body:
Let's say Counterfact generates a GET function and a POST function in /paths/pets.ts

We change the GET function but leave the POST function alone. After making a change to the OpenAPI document, we want to recreate all generated code without overwriting manually edited code. 

For that reason, Counterfact currently will not touch any file under paths if a file already exists. 

Instead of ignoring the file completely, ideally it would leave the GET function alone and recreate the POST function. 

To make this work, we can create an index file which keeps track of all generated functions and hashes of their ASTs. If a given function already exists, but it's hash has not changed, we know it's safe to recreate that function. Otherwise leave it alone. 

Theoretically this same logic could be applied to other files, allowing users to make changes to the generated types if they so desire. I don't think we should encourage that behavior but it could be an option that's off by default.

items.body:
Similar to #86 

For testing purpose, I would like to make access runtime access to the `context` object at the heart of a server as convenient as possible. Why not expose it through the browser's dev tools?

Not necessarily _direct_ access. What I'm thinking is we create a proxy context object that runs in the browser, with method signatures matching the context object on the server. When you call `context.reticulate('splines')` on the browser object, it sends the method name and arguments to the server via a web socket. Counterfact then intercepts that request on the server side and calls `context.reticulate('splines')` on the server object. The return value is then `JSON.stringify()`ed and returned to the client. 

Two consequences of this remote procedure call (RPC) approach:

1. It only works on methods that take JSON-serializable objects as arguments and return JSON-serializable values. Maybe we can use TypeScript to enforce that _all_ context methods follow this convention. That feels like a good idea anyway, as it will encourage people to move business logic into the `Context` class instead of the `/paths/**/*.ts` files. 

3. Every method on the client-side context object is asynchronous. If we care about the return value we need to use `await x = context.reticulate('splines')` even if the `reticulate()` method is synchronous on the server side.

items.body:
Given the following schema:

```yaml
type: object
  additionalProperties:
    type: integer
```

SchemaTypeCoder should yield the following type:

```ts
{
    [k: string]: number
}
```

However, given the following schema.

```yaml
type: object
  properties:
    name: firstName
    type: string 
  additionalProperties:
    type: integer
```

All properties _except_ name should be numbers. [TypeScript currently has no way to represent an object with some properties that have one type and all other properties of another type.](
https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/issues/17867) The best we can do is this:

```ts
{
    name?: string
    [k: string]: unknown
}
```

It also needs to handle the case where `additionalProperties` is `true` or `false`.

Now that I've written it out I realize it boils down to something like this.

```js

if (hasAdditionalProperties) {
    if(hasProperties) {
       append('[k: string]: unknown')
    } else {
       append(`[k: string]: ${additionalProperties.type}`)
    } 
}
```

I don't really care about this case at this point, but if ALL of the properties happen to have the same type as `additionalProperties`, then we can resolve the type instead of putting `unknown` in.

items.body:
I'm looking for a **web component** that renders a widget with a dropdown for request method, a text box for URL, and a button to fetch the URL. Clicking the button invokes a request and renders the response below. 

Code:

```html
<api-widget methods="GET,POST" url="/hello/world">
```

Output:

```
[GET v] [/hello/world        ] [Go]
```

```
[POST v] [/hello/world       ] [Go]
Request body:
----------------------------------
|                                |
|                                |
|                                |
|                                |
|                                |
----------------------------------
```



After clicking the "Go" button:

```
[GET v] [/hello/world       ] [Go]
Response:
----------------------------------
| HTTP/2 200 Ok                  |
| Connection: Closed             |
| Content-Type: application/json |
|                                |                               
|                                |
| {                              |
|   message: "hello world"       |
| }                              |
----------------------------------
```


It doesn't have to be an exact replica of what I described. Anything that roughly fits the description and is implemented as a web component will do. 

I want it to use in the documentation. It has nothing to do with Counterfact per se. If there's not already something out there, I'm hoping someone will go build one and release it as a separate npm package that Counterfact can import.

While Counterfact generates TypeScript, Counterfact itself was originally written in JavaScript. The server code is now in TypeScript. Now just need to update the typescript-generator code.

## REPL

Finalize the API for `.proxy`: `.proxy [on|off [path]]`, `.proxy set url`

## Server

### Add the Open API document to $

The particular use case I have in mind is being able to pass a schema to json-schema-faker, so that we can exercise fine-grained control over what is generated.

items.body:
Counterfact was originally intended to solve some of the same problems as the items listed on this page:

https://mswjs.io/docs/comparison

Now it's also taken on generating TypeScript code from OpenAPI. Because I couldn't find anything that generates TypeScript code that I found to be sufficiently readable and easy to relate back to the source.

https://openapi-generator.tech/docs/generators/

And I have some other big ideas that I haven't written down yet, like building automated acceptance tests, fiddling with the server's state via a REPL, and building some kind of IDE plugin to trace a type back to its source in the Open API spec.

labels.name: archive
labels.description: Mostly Patrick brainstorming in the early days

milestone.title: Future
milestone.description: Future enhancements that are not (yet) tied to any upcoming release

items.body:
The TypeScript generator might be easier to read, maintain, and test if it built up ASTs rather cobbling strings together with template literals. 

A couple of libraries we could use:

- https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/Using-the-Compiler-API
- https://github.com/dsherret/ts-morph

It can be done one `Coder` at a time and we may decided part of the way through that it's not a good idea. The first step is to implement the base `Coder#write()` method like so:

```
write(script) {
    return printer.print(this.buildAst(script)); 
}
```

Then within each subclass create a `buildAst()` method and delete the `write()` method.

The particular use case I have in mind is being able to pass a schema to json-schema-faker, so that we can exercise fine-grained control over what is generated.

```ts

```

items.body:
The word "path" in this codebase can mean a few different things:

- a file path
- a path in the tree structure of a JSON / YAML file
- node's built-in path module

To ease the confusion, everywhere we import path, the code should be:

```js
import nodePath from "node:path";
```

Avoid these patterns:

```js
import path from "node:path";
import { join } from "node:path"; 
```

items.title: Point Counterfact to a JS file rather than a directory

milestone.title: Future
milestone.description: Future enhancements that are not (yet) tied to any upcoming release

items.body:
Currently the base path is expected to be a directory.

```
my-app
   /routes <-- here
      /articles
         /[articleId].js
      /categories.js
```

However, the base path could be a file. 
```
my-app
   /routes
      /articles
         /[articleId].js
      /categories.js
   /routes.js <-- here
```

And that makes a lot of sense, because that top level file could implement default handlers for each of the request methods.

items.title: parameterized paths

milestone.title: MVP
milestone.description:
- obvious functionality such as reading / writing headers 
- sufficient unit test coverage
- documentation  
- metadata in package.json

items.body:
Sometimes a parameter appears in the middle of a path, e.g.:

```
/users/{user_id}/profile
/users/{user_id}/friends
/users/{user_id}/preferences
```

The filesystem based routing scheme doesn't currently accommodate this use case well. Ideally we would model the above like so:

```
- users
   - user_id
       - friends.js
       - preferences.js
       - profile.js
 ```
  

But that will only match these URLs

```
/users/user_id/friends
/users/user_id/preferences
/users/user_id/profile
 ```

Whereas we want it to match URLs that look like this:

```
/users/12345/friends
/users/12345/preferences
/users/12345/profile

/users/86753/friends
/users/86753/preferences
/users/86753/profile

/users/99999/friends
/users/99999/preferences
/users/99999/profile
```

We need a way to identify that the `user_id` directory is a wildcard, not meant to be matched literally. Where would be the right place to encode that information? How about in `user.js`?

```
- users
   - user_id
       - friends.js
       - preferences.js
       - profile.js
- users.js <--- here
 ```

```js
// users.js 
const USER_ID_REGEX = /^\d{3,10}$/;

export function wildcard(key) {
   if(USER_ID_REGEX.test(key) { 
       return 'user_id';
   } 
   return key;
}
```

When parsing the URL `/users/99999/profile`, Counterfact will look at users.js and find that it has a wildcard function. Since "99999" is a valid user ID, it will next look for `./users/user_id.js` and `./users/user_id/profile.js` instead of `./users/99999.js` and `./users/99999/profile.js`

Profile.js will then look something like this:
```js
//profile.js

export function GET({path, store}) {
   return {
      body: `User profile for ${path.user_id}: ${store.users[path.user_id].profile}`
   }
}

export function PUT({path, store, body}) {
    store.users[path.user_id].profile = body;
   return {
      body: `ok`
   }
}

```
